#312. The advantages of using a USB-C docking station

Plus, there are differences between a USB-C hub and a docking station.

Laptops have been getting thinner and lighter from year to year, and they have become so powerful that many people choose a laptop as their main computer. But a thin body means fewer ports, and a desktop setup with a screen, mouse, webcam and keyboard requires a lot of them. If you have a laptop and still want the full desktop experience, a USB-C docking station can be the solution you're looking for.

A USB-C docking station is a box that connects to your laptop through a single USB-C cable and gives it a full set of ports. USB-C docking stations reduce cord clutter, add more ports to your setup and can keep your laptop's own ports from wearing down.

The biggest advantage of a dock is simplicity. One single cable connects the laptop to its peripherals. That means you can come home and plug in all your devices with one plug; you can also grab your laptop on your way out just as quickly. Monitors, a keyboard, a webcam and a charger no longer need to be reconnected every time the laptop comes and goes, and your desk stays tidier because the cables run to the dock instead of the laptop.

A dock can also add ports your laptop doesn't have. Depending on the model, you can get HDMI or DisplayPort outputs for external monitors, more USB ports, an SD card reader and an Ethernet port for a stable wired internet connection. A thin laptop that comes with three or four ports can end up with a dozen.

The third advantage is less wear on your laptop. Plugging and unplugging several cables over and over puts strain on the ports, and a dock takes that job over. Instead of plugging several cables into the laptop every day, you plug in just one.

If you only need a few basic connections, a USB-C hub is the cheaper option. Hubs have roughly four to 10 ports and cost anywhere between $30 and $150. Docking stations generally have more ports, come with their own DC power adapter, and cost more, with some higher-end models costing more than $400. A dock can give you a full desktop setup with multiple monitors, plus more ports of every kind, and the higher-end Thunderbolt 4 and USB4 models can run multiple displays, Ethernet, audio and laptop charging through that one cable. If that sounds like what you need, here are the best docking stations for laptops.

Before buying, it's worth checking a few things, because not every dock works with every laptop. A USB-C port only outputs video if it supports DisplayPort Alt Mode or is a Thunderbolt or USB4 port, and the dock needs to support Power Delivery pass-through at your laptop's required wattage. If you plan to work with the lid closed, keep the power plugged in, since the laptop draws more power with an external monitor attached.

Get those details right and a dock quietly does its job, providing a laptop that goes back to being portable by unplugging just one cable.

#311. Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines

“We don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price…”

When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.

“We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday. “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”

If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025, with additional price hikes happening this year.

For the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year. And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad said.

While Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the company was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.

For now, at least, Valve says it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The company now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.

Valve says it plans to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.

#310. Study finds slightly higher risk of autism diagnosis in areas with more lithium in drinking water, but experts say more research is needed

A new study found a moderately higher risk of autism spectrum disorder in children born to pregnant people exposed to tap water with higher levels of lithium, but experts caution that this association does not show a direct link between the two.

About 1 in 36 children in the US is diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) each year, according to data from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Scientists still don’t know the exact cause of autism, a developmental disorder. Genetics may be a factor, but some have been looking at potential environmental causes, too.

Autism diagnosis has become more common, but pandemic disrupted early detection, CDC says

Cases may be on the rise, but that is also unclear. One study published this year on cases in the New York-New Jersey area found that autism diagnosis rates tripled among certain age groups between 2000 and 2016. A 2021 report found similar increases in cases, but the CDC says the increased number of cases is most likely linked to more doctors screening for the condition.

Lithium is an alkali metal that can be found naturally in some food and ground water. It’s used in batteries, grease and air conditioners, as well as in the treatment of bipolar disorder and some blood disorders. Its levels in US drinking water are not regulated, according to the US Geological Survey.

A new study, published Monday in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, found a small association between lithium and autism diagnosis in Denmark, where the researchers say the level of lithium in drinking water is similar to that in American water systems.

The researchers checked a database of people with psychiatric disorders for children born between 2000 and 2013 to find information on 8,842 cases of ASD and 43,864 participants who did not have ASD. They then measured the concentration of lithium in 151 public waterworks that served more than half of the Danish population and mapped out where pregnant people lived in relation.

For many neurodiverse people, 'The Sims' has been a lifelong comfort

As lithium levels in water increased, there was a modest increased risk of an ASD diagnosis. Specifically, compared with people at the lowest exposure level, those who had the second and third highest exposure during pregnancy had a 24% to 26% higher risk of ASD diagnosed in children. The group with the highest exposure had a 46% higher risk than those at the lowest level of exposure.

The researchers could not tell how much water the pregnant people drank, but they picked Denmark in part because residents there consume some of the lowest amounts of bottled water in Europe.

Experts say it’s important to note that the research can’t show that lithium exposure leads directly to an autism diagnosis.

Further study is required, said study co-author Dr. Beate Ritz, a professor of neurology in the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and a professor of epidemiology and environmental health at the UCLA Fielding School of Public Health.

“Any drinking water contaminants that may affect the developing human brain deserve intense scrutiny,” Ritz said in a news release. She added that the research would need to be replicated in other countries to look for a similar connection.

The implications of the findings are complex as far as public health policy is concerned, according to an editorial published alongside the study. Lithium levels in water, at concentrations that the study associated with a potential ASD risk, have also been linked with health benefits such as lower rates of hospitalization for psychiatric disorders and suicide.

“If all these of associations are valid, the wisdom of Solomon will be required to develop guidelines for lithium in drinking water that are maximally protective of the entire population,” wrote Dr. David C. Bellinger, a professor of neurology and psychology at Harvard Medical School. “Until the basic biology of ASD is better understood, it will be difficult to distinguish causal from spurious associations.”

'Heartbreaking' delays in autism diagnosis and treatment got even worse during pandemic

Dr. Max Wiznitzer, director of the Rainbow Autism Center at University Hospitals Rainbow Babies and Children’s Hospital in Cleveland, points to other research on the effects of lithium on pregnant people who take it for mental health disorders. Those studies – which look at people exposed to much higher levels than are found in drinking water – do not show a connection with autism spectrum disorder.

“It’s an interesting association, but causation is definitely not proven,” said Wiznitzer, who was not involved in the new research. “We have to see if there’s a viable and biologically plausible mechanism by which a small amount of lithium in the water supply can somehow do this, yet pharmacologic dosing of lithium in women with bipolar disorder has not been reported to be causing increased risk of ASD.”

Other studies have also suggested connections between ASD and environmental exposures to things like pesticides, air pollution and phthalates. But none of them points to any of these factors as a direct cause of the disorder.

Sign up here to get The Results Are In with Dr. Sanjay Gupta every Tuesday from the CNN Health team.

A link between environmental exposure and ASD is hard to prove, Wiznitzer said. With research showing that increased exposure to air pollution raises the risk of giving birth to a child with ASD, for example, he often wonders whether pollution is the determining factor or if it’s just the populations who live in more polluted areas.

“There’s a lot of speculation about about environmental factors, but how many of them are truly causally associated?” Wiznitzer said. “We are bombarded with a variety of environmental stressors in our everyday lives. We have to figure out how to basically safely navigate them, and this is probably not one that’s high on our list.”

#309. You don't need a foldable phone to use split screen on Android

Despite all odds, folding smartphones have stuck around. They've mostly found their place in two  categories: flip phones that fold a regular-sized smartphone in half for portability and book-style phones that unfold to reveal a larger canvas. For years, foldables like the Galaxy Z Fold 8 have been marketed as productivity machines, allowing you to get more things done on a device you carry around in your pocket. Split screen multitasking is often highlighted as one of their biggest selling points, but you don't need to set aside close to $2,000 just to use two apps at the same time.

Split screen multitasking has been around since Android 7.0 Nougat, which was released a decade ago in 2016. In fact, the feature was first discovered in Android 6.0 Marshmallow, though it required root access. All modern Android smartphones should come with this multitasking feature out of the box, but the exact steps to activate it might differ depending on your phone's manufacturer and Android version. Most phones, including ones from Google, Samsung and Motorola, let you enable split screen multitasking through the recent apps switcher.

This can be accessed by swiping up from the very bottom and holding on the screen if you're using gesture navigation, or by tapping the Recents button if you use the three-button navigation system. All of your opened apps will be listed here. Tap on an app's icon and select Split Screen from the options that show up. You can now select a second app that you want open alongside the first one. You can further adjust how much space each app occupies by dragging the divider in the middle. Dragging it all the way up or down will exit the split screen mode.

Most traditional slab-style Android phones only let you use a maximum of two apps at once in split screen view — not that you'd realistically want to cram a third one onto such a small display anyway. This is where larger foldables let you take multitasking a step further by accommodating three or more apps at the same time. That said, split screen view isn't the only multitasking feature that Android offers.

Modern Android phones also let you use apps in floating windows, which allows for a slightly different kind of multitasking. Instead of splitting your screen in two halves, a floating window appears on top of whatever app you're currently using. This lets you view and interact with two apps simultaneously without splitting the screen. You can move the floating window around or resize it by grabbing its edges or corners.

Different manufacturers handle this feature differently. Pixel phones running Android 17, for instance, offer the Bubbles feature, which lets you use floating apps that collapse into Facebook Messenger-style chat heads when minimized, allowing you to open them quickly without leaving your current app. Samsung calls this feature Pop-up view while some manufacturers like OnePlus and Oppo simply label it Floating Windows.

ColorOS 17 handles it particularly well, even allowing you to change the aspect ratio of certain floating windows. My OnePlus 15 can accommodate two apps in split screen view and a third one running in a floating window on top, though I'm yet to find a use case that warrants this level of multitasking madness on a slab-style phone.

Though the feature has been around for a hot minute, you may find the split view mode not working in some cases. App compatibility has improved a lot over the years, but there are still a few apps that might not work in multiwindow setups. When this is the case, you'll either find the Split View option greyed out or simply missing. It's still worth heading to the Play Store and updating all of your apps to see if an app's newer version might introduce support for split screen multitasking.

If not, this is Android we're talking about, so of course there's a workaround. Hidden away in the Developer Options menu is the Force activities to be resizable toggle. Turning this on might let you force split screen mode for apps that don't officially support it. This might not always work, though. For instance, it seemed to do the trick for all unsupported apps on my older Android phone, but I didn't have the same luck on my current device. There's also no guarantee that unsupported apps will play nicely in split screen view.

The Developer Options menu is hidden by default. To enable it, navigate to Settings > About, look for the Build Number entry and tap on it seven times. Enter your PIN or password when prompted. Once enabled, you can find the hidden menu under Settings > System on most phones. While simply having Developer Options enabled isn't inherently dangerous, it does hold many advanced settings that might affect your phone's performance and stability, so it's best to leave anything you're not familiar with unchanged.

#307. COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the plans to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment."

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

#306. Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

Modeling predicts plume of neurotoxic lead could reach up to 100 miles away.

In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

“Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”

Telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”

Lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army said. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”

In an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army said that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”

The military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it said the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

In all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” plan the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army said the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”

According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the plan is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

The Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

Modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

During the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed.  It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

The Army’s plan was to communicate clearly with the public about the plans, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

In its environmental risk assessment, the Army said it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”

Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the plan.

“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

On Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the plan “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting plans until it can review the case.

Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:

The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”

This post was updated November 20 to include that the federal appeals court granted a stay in the case brought by the environmental groups.

#305. What the tiny key icon means on your Android device

The Android status bar is designed to give users important information at a glance, but all those icons can blur together. One of the most unusual symbols looks like a leftward-facing key with two teeth opposite its circular handle. That icon tells you that your internet connection is encrypted, but there's nothing to worry about.

More specifically, that icon is a visual indicator that you're connected via a VPN that encrypts your web traffic from third parties. Many people consider a VPN crucial for their online security, and modern Android versions support VPNs at the OS level. The key icon, then, lets users know they're safe behind their VPN, while its absence alerts them that their encryption has been broken, giving them a chance to address it.

The key icon appears only when a VPN is active, so the only way to get rid of it is to disable the VPN. If you're running a third-party VPN, open the app and turn it off from there. Some VPN apps even keep a notification active with a button to turn them off, making it an even quicker process. On a Pixel or other close-to-stock Android device, you can also swipe into Quick Settings and tap the number next to the profile icon at the bottom of the screen to show active background apps, then tap Stop next to your VPN.

If you don't know which VPN you're running, open your phone's Settings app and go to Network & internet > VPN, then tap on it from the list there. On Samsung Galaxy phones, go to Settings > Connections > More connection settings > VPN to find a functionally identical screen. If you are connected to a VPN, it will be shown on a list with text underneath reading "Connected." Tap the running VPN and choose Disconnect. If you are not connected to a VPN, tap a VPN, and you will be taken to its app, where you can connect.

Tapping the settings gear icon next to any VPN will allow you to configure it further. If you want to configure a VPN manually, you can tap the plus icon in the top right, but this is generally recommended for advanced users. For more, see our guide on how to use a VPN. All other aspects of your VPN can be managed within its proprietary app. Since every VPN has a different interface in its app, consult your provider's documentation if you're not sure how to use a feature or setting.

Another classic use case is making it appear as though you are somewhere you're not, usually to access geofenced content. For instance, Netflix may offer shows in other countries that it doesn't in your own due to licensing deals, and a VPN will let you set your location to those regions to access that content.

While VPNs offer benefits, they can cause issues when browsing the web. Some websites will treat your device as inherently suspicious when it connects from a VPN IP address, and you may encounter more anti-automation measures such as CAPTCHAs. Some websites may even be totally unresponsive until you disconnect your VPN. Despite that, if you already pay for a service that includes a VPN, it may be worth enabling it to get a taste of what using a VPN is like on your phone. Otherwise, have a gander at our list of the best VPNs in 2026.

#304. Syrian refugee elected mayor of German town, years after fleeing war

A Syrian who arrived in Germany as a refugee in 2015 has won a mayoral election in the southwestern German state of Baden-Württemberg.

Ryyan Alshebl, who left his hometown of As Suwayda in Syria eight years ago, ran as an independent in the municipality of Ostelsheim. He won 55.41% of the votes on Sunday, beating two German candidates, Marco Strauss and Mathias Fey.

Locals cheered the 29-year-old when he welcomed his win, a victory he described as “sensational,” German local broadcaster SWR reported Monday.

“Today, Ostelsheim sent an example for broad-mindedness and cosmopolitanism for the whole of Germany,” he said, according to to German public broadcaster ZDF. “That’s not something that can be taken for granted in a conservative, rural area.”

Alshebl’s first call after his victory was to his mother in Syria, who was thrilled with the news, SWR reported.

The Association of Municipalities of Baden-Württemberg said Alshebl is the first man with Syrian roots to run for and win a mayor’s office. He will start his role in June.

'You are not a refugee.' Roma refugees fleeing war in Ukraine say they are suffering discrimination and prejudice

Ostelsheim residents have welcomed their incoming mayor. “The fairy tale has come true, and the right man has become our mayor,” Annette Keck, who lives in the village, told SWR.

Strauss, one of his opponents, congratulated Alshebl. “I wish you good luck and at the same time ask for support for Mr. Alshebl, for our shared Ostelsheim,” he said on Facebook.

The state’s Integration Minister Manne Lucha said that Alshebl’s victory showed that diversity is a natural part of Baden-Württemberg. “I would be very pleased if Ryyan Alshebl’s election encourages more people with a migration history to run for political office,” he said.

Not everyone has been so warm to the 29-year-old. ZDF reported the Syrian received hateful comments on the campaign trail.

The young politician went from house to house, promoting his election program, and “the experiences were predominantly positive,” but there was also a minority of far-right fringe voters in Ostelsheim that did not want to accept him due to his Syrian roots, Alshebl told ZDF.

Born to a schoolteacher and agricultural engineer in Syria, Alshebl described his life as carefree until the age of 20, according to his campaign website.

At the time, protests against the Syrian government that began in 2011 soon devolved into chaotic war. The fighting and later rise of ISIS forced 10.6 million people from home by late 2015 – about half of Syria’s pre-war population.

Alshebl faced the dilemma of being drafted for military service with the Syrian army or leaving the country, according to his website.

While many Syrians were displaced internally or fled to countries in the region, others like Alshebl made the dangerous journey to Europe. He was 21 years old at the time, and said he crossed from Turkey to the Greek island of Lesbos in a rubber dinghy.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel had implemented a brief open-door policy in 2015 that saw the country take in about 1.2 million asylum seekers in the following years, including Alshebl.

They were welcomed into British homes. Celebrating their first Christmas together, Ukrainians wonder if that hospitality will last

The move sparked a backlash in Germany and the sudden growth of the far-right, anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the wake of summer 2015.

Once in Germany, Alshebl lived close to Ostelsheim and said at the time he felt “there is only one thing you can do: get back on your feet quickly and start investing in your own future quickly.”

For the last seven years he worked in the administration of Althengstett town hall, in a neighboring town. He drew from his experience, he said in his campaign, and made digital access to to public administration services one of priorities. Flexible childcare and climate protections are also on his agenda.

Alshebl, who is a member of the Green Party and now has German citizenship, pledged during his campaign that once elected as mayor he would move to Ostelsheim.

#303. These iOS settings will help you control your mobile data use

Avoid data overage charges or speed thorttling with these iOS settings.

Cellular connectivity is now fast and reliable enough to rival home broadband, especially with 5G. But telcos typically aren't as generous about data allowances. If you don't watch your data use, you may end up with hefty bills — if your telco charges for excess data — or painfully slow speeds once you exceed your monthly allowance. You consume cellular data not just when you're downloading a file or watching a video, either: background app refresh, app updates and cloud syncing can also eat into your data allowance bit by bit.

The iPhone offers a handful of built-in settings that can help you monitor and manage mobile data use. Firstly, you can view a list of apps and how much data they use by heading to Settings > Cellular, scrolling down to the Cellular Data section and tapping on Show All. This will list mobile data use for individual apps you have installed. You can sort these apps by name or usage to quickly identify which ones consume the most data.

Tap the toggle next to any app to prevent it from using cellular data. The app will stop updating its content in the background when you're not connected to Wi-Fi and might also stop sending you notifications. The next time you launch the app, it will alert you that mobile data has been turned off for the app and give you the option to re-enable it.

If you rely mainly on Wi-Fi, turning off mobile data can prevent data usage and reduce battery drain. Navigate to Settings > Cellular to toggle Cellular Data on or off. iOS also lets you limit data consumption, so you can keep cellular data on without exhausting your monthly allowance as quickly. In Cellular settings, navigate to Cellular Data Options > Data Mode and select Low Data Mode. This setting might be set to Standard by default, which allows automatic updates and background tasks even when you're not on Wi-Fi. Low Data Mode restricts this, reducing your mobile data use.

Being connected to Wi-Fi doesn't guarantee that your iPhone won't consume mobile data. Head to Settings > Wi-Fi, scroll down and turn the Connectivity Assist toggle off. Before iOS 27, this feature was called Wi-Fi Assist and could be found under Settings > Cellular. The feature keeps your iPhone constantly connected to the internet, but it uses mobile data to do so. When a Wi-Fi connection becomes too weak or busy, Connectivity Assist switches to cellular data to keep you connected to the internet. If you don't mind potential disruptions, turning this feature off may reduce unexpected mobile data use.

Beyond the Settings app, there are other ways you can restrict mobile data use on your iPhone. For starters, changing automatic update behavior can help avoid unexpected cellular activity. Navigate to Settings > Apps > App Store and, under the Mobile Data section, turn the Automatic Downloads toggle off. Open the Settings app, tap on your name at the top, navigate to iCloud > iCloud Backup and make sure the Back Up Over Mobile Data toggle is unchecked.

If you stream music regularly, check the audio quality in your app of choice. Apple Music users can find this option by navigating to Settings > Apps > Music > Audio Quality > Data Streaming. Lossless audio may provide a superior listening experience, but it is an absolute data hog. Other apps, like Tidal, Spotify and YouTube Music, also let you reduce audio quality when using mobile data. Lowering video quality to 720p on YouTube can also help manage data consumption. You can also reduce how much data your navigation apps use by downloading maps for offline use; both Apple Maps and Google Maps let you do so.

Lastly, you can look for toggles and features in third-party apps designed to reduce cellular usage. For instance, you can stop WhatsApp from automatically downloading media from new chats by tapping your profile picture, navigating to Storage and data and setting the Media auto-download option for photos, videos and documents to Wi-Fi. Instagram fans can find a Use less mobile data toggle by opening the app's settings page and navigating to Media quality.

#302. Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 23, 2026

Tomorrow marks the Full Moon, but tonight's Moon already looks almost full. It's still technically in its Waxing Gibbous phase, with just a small portion of its surface left in the darkness.

As of Monday, Nov. 23, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 97% of its surface visible.

If you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Tranquillitatis and Fecunditatis, as well as the Aristarchus Plateau. With binoculars, you'll also see the Grimaldi Basin, the Endymion Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 11, 15, and 16 landing spots.

The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

According to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a New Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

New Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

First Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

Waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere)

Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

Lois Mackenzie is a freelance reporter at Mashable. Over the years she has written for many publications, covering everything from the local news to the best pair of running shoes. You can find bylines in publications including Fit&Well, Metro, and Coach magazine, usually covering deals on everything from earbuds to TVs, or guides on how to beat your half marathon time.

Lois also holds a Master's degree in Digital Journalism from Strathclyde University and obtained a Master of Arts in English Literature at the University of Aberdeen.

#301. How Secure Is Your Password? Here's How To Test It

Here’s what a strong password looks like and how to check whether yours would hold up against hackers, plus a few habits that keep accounts safer.

Remember the old days when you'd try to use "1234" or "password" as your password? There really was never a time when passwords like those were secure. Thankfully, nowadays, most services don't even permit you to use passwords that aren't secure enough. They require a combination of letters, numbers and symbols along with different letter cases before accepting your chosen password. It makes passwords tougher to remember on the one hand, but it's essential in this day and age to ensure that your password can't be easily cracked by nefarious individuals or even AI systems.

But even if you think you have created a password that Robert Langdon from The Da Vinci Code himself couldn't crack, how do you truly know how secure it is? Usually, if it includes all the elements noted above, especially if the letters do not connect to spell an actual word, you're in a good spot.

To know for sure, you can run it through a free password strength checker, such as the one at Security.org. However, remember that creating a secure password is just one of the steps you can take to be safer online.

It's important to understand what makes a good password in the first place. It should be at least 12 characters, and in fact, many sites do not let you submit a password that is less than that anyway. Along with the aforementioned upper and lower case letters, numbers and symbols, keep in mind that the letters should not spell a discernible, and certainly not an identifiable word like your surname. They should also not be consecutive in the alphabet, like "LMNOP," or in a row on a keyboard, like "QWERTY." The same goes for numbers, which should be random instead of something like your birthday or street address. The letters and numbers should not be repeated as well, like "BBB" or "555."

Once you create a password you think is secure, enter it into the Security.org checker, which evaluates it and provides feedback. As you type, the site shows how long it would take a computer to crack the password. The more characters you add, the longer this duration becomes. I went from a password with letters and numbers that would take four years to figure out to one with symbols that bumps it to 2 million years before someone could crack it. It's safe to say both are secure, but the latter is more secure. When I tried using a simple word with consecutive numbers, it advised that the password could be cracked in three days.

When creating an account, you might see an option to "create a strong password" automatically after which you can save it to password memory, like Apple MacBook's Passwords app or a third-party password manager like 1Password. It's a good idea to use these even over signing in with an existing Google, Apple or other account. There are convenience benefits to doing that, but for extra security, create a new login.

If this automatic password creation option isn't offered, you can use third-party services like LastPass to generate a strong password. For an extra layer of security, you can also add an authenticator app like Google Authenticator, which generates a six-digit code that continuously changes. After entering your password, you're asked to input the appropriate code given by the authenticator app every time you log in, making the account even tougher to crack. But this two-factor authentication method isn't always available.

There are pros and cons of using a password manager over an authenticator app, but there's no reason you can't use both. If the site offers passkeys versus passwords, these are worth using. They can be more secure, relying on a private key accessed through biometrics (your fingerprint or face) or a PIN.

Along with having a secure password, it is also important to make every password unique. If you use the same password for everything, no matter how secure, what happens if someone gains access to it from one account? This could happen through a breach or even human error, and it would unlock all your accounts and services. Keeping passwords secure and unique to every service and changing them every 60 to 90 days or immediately if a breach has been reported will keep you as safe as possible.

#300. Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.

CTIA said jamming test showed “interference… up to two and a half miles away.”

The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:

The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA said the pilot test shows “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”

The FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”

The Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC says its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

Carr said that “contraband cell phones continue to pour into prisons by the thousands each year,” with “estimates indicat[ing] that as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to these devices.” He said the phones have been used to plan scams, drug trafficking, and violent attacks.

“In Georgia, an incarcerated gang leader directed a drive-by shooting that killed two 13-year-old boys at a birthday party,” Carr said, referring to a 2024 shooting.

Carr defended the plan against criticism that it will block legitimate communications outside the prisons, saying it includes safeguards to prevent that.

“Those that want to use the technology will apply to the FCC, explain how they plan to deploy it, and show through testing that it stays inside the designated area and doesn’t interfere with lawful communications outside the prison walls,” Carr said. “Communities nearby will receive notice before operations start. We’re also seeking comment on next steps, including ways to close remaining loopholes on other frequencies and the possibility of quiet zones around correctional facilities.”

Freedom of the Press Foundation Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern said the FCC should have considered the benefits of contraband phones being used to document abuses inside prisons.

“Prisons are the most secretive government institutions in the country and people wishing to expose abuses and inhumane conditions from the inside often do not have many options,” Stern wrote in a letter to FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez’s office, which was included on the FCC docket. “Last year’s Oscar-nominated film, The Alabama Solution, used footage incarcerated people captured with contraband cell phones to show Americans some of the awful things that go on in state prisons that they’d have no other way of seeing. The same footage bolstered an ongoing DOJ investigation into Alabama prisons and was crucial evidence in a civil lawsuit by Steven Davis, who was brutally killed by prison guards, that eventually settled.”

Jamming contraband cellphones was supported by prison phone companies ViaPath (aka Global Tel*Link) and NCIC Correctional Services, the National District Attorneys Association, the Correctional Leaders Association, and National Association of Police Organizations.

“Inmates have used these phones to coordinate attacks against correctional officers and their families, as well as inmate violence, strikes, disturbances, and full-scale riots,” the National Association of Police Organizations said. “They also use contraband phones to organize deliveries of illegal drugs and weapons into correctional facilities. These dangers underscore the need to authorize indoor jamming in state and local correctional facilities.”

Gomez, the only Democrat on the three-member commission, said she’s concerned about potential unintended consequences, but voted with Republicans to allow jamming after safeguards were added to the order.

“For the last 90 years, the Federal Communications Commission has prohibited jamming by non-federal actors and even prohibited jamming equipment to be introduced into the American market,” Gomez said. “That is because jamming devices are specifically designed to interfere with communications devices in order to render them un-usable.”

Gomez said that “jamming can prevent devices from completing 911 and emergency calls as well as interfere with communications networks used by fire, police, Emergency Medical Services, and other public safety entities.” She also said making jamming equipment available in the American market could lead to “unauthorized sale of this hazardous equipment,” and that “the accessibility of jamming equipment can itself motivate criminal enterprise.” Criminals have used “Wi-Fi jammers to disrupt security systems, security cameras, and cellphones to conduct robberies at homes and at stores,” she said.

Gomez said she’s glad the final order includes safeguards “to ensure that jamming is contained to this unique use, to permit jamming by a very limited category of authorized actors, and to take as much care as possible to prevent jamming and jamming equipment from becoming a hazard to safety.”

Gomez partially dissented because she is worried the FCC will let correctional facilities and prison phone companies charge higher prices for inmate calling services that connect inmates with family members. Under US law, the FCC sets limits on those prices and considers prisons’ and jails’ safety and security costs when deciding how much money they can charge, she said.

Gomez said, “While correctional facilities should have safety and security services like jamming to prevent criminal activity, it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay for the costs of these measures… Jamming is specifically designed to block communications and is certainly not necessary to provide phone and video calls for incarcerated individuals. We should have made this clear in today’s order. Because we failed to do so, I dissent in part.”

The FCC order could be challenged in court. The CTIA has argued that the FCC “has no authority to allow jamming” under the Communications Act, which directs the FCC to prevent interference.

AT&T said the FCC’s legal justification “is premised on a fundamental factual error: the assumption that jammers will only block ‘unauthorized’ communications without impacting lawful uses. There is no way to jam some communications on a spectrum band but not others. That is because radio jammers ‘block all wireless communications on affected spectrum bands,’ and, as the FCC has noted in the past, ‘cannot differentiate between contraband devices and legitimate devices.’”

AT&T said that “there is simply no way to limit the reach of jammers to the confines of a given facility. Jammers have been shown to cause interference outside the facilities in which they operate, greatly increasing the risk that someone living or traveling nearby will be impacted.”

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#299. Hurdle hints and answers for November 23, 2026

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

#298. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#297. Which solar panel type is best for your home?

More efficient solar panels aren't always the better buy. Your roof, budget and plans for backup power have a say too.

At first glance, all the solar panels in your neighborhood may look much the same, but what they're made of can decide how much power they generate. Monocrystalline panels tend to generate more power per square foot compared to older polycrystalline models. And when skylights, chimneys and vents already take up some of the sunniest spots, picking the right solar panel can matter.

But just because a certain panel technology is more efficient doesn't instantly make it the best choice. External factors like your electricity consumption, how much shade the panels get and what your utility pays for surplus energy can change the math considerably, so it can pay to size your system using the 20 percent rule for solar panels. That means building in enough capacity to produce around 20 percent more energy than your household normally uses as a buffer for dimmer days. At the same time, inverters, mounting hardware and labor for installing the equipment need to be accounted for too (no matter how compelling the brochure seems).

There's also the burning question of what you'll be powering up with those solar panels. Someone hoping to shave off some bucks on their monthly bill needs a different setup from one who needs their Wi-Fi and kitchen appliances to survive the next power outage.

Between the monocrystalline cells (built from a single crystal of silicon) and polycrystalline cells, the former do pack a higher power density. These polycrystalline panels could be cheaper where they're still available, but they also take up more space to produce comparable power. Thin-film panels, on the other hand, are built from thin layers of photovoltaic material, and while some are flexible and light enough for unconventional mounting, they're hardly ever the first choice for a traditional pitched roof.

Modern monocrystalline panels come with cell technologies like TOPCon, HJT and PERC, just to name a few. While most of these aren't based on entirely new materials, each has its own merits for boosting overall cell performance. Let's take Qcells' n-type Q.TRON BLK M-G2+, for instance, which can deliver 440W at 22.5 percent module efficiency, while Tesla's 420W residential module is at least 20.5 percent efficient. Of course, it wouldn't be a fair comparison without factoring in the size of the panels, but neither vendor's specifications alone can give you a breakdown of how much power the panels will pump out for your specific roof.

And it isn't entirely dependent on sunlight either, since solar panels tend to become less efficient as they get warmer. Plus, factors like shading and orientation of the panels can also make a sizable dent in the annual output. Sure, bifacial panels do exist for capturing reflected light from the back end, but this benefit is mostly dependent on how they are mounted, along with the environment.

Now, before you sign up for anything, take a long minute to understand those installation quotes and what you're getting for your money. The right way to do this is to compare projected annual electricity production and total expense rather than the wattage printed on the modules. Those details, like roof repairs, permits, inverters and warranty coverage, can make the quote comparison quite the ordeal.

To give you some context, the Solar Energy Industries Association reported that the price of an average US residential installation was $3.36 per watt in the second quarter of 2026. For perspective, one of our editors spent just over $24,000 on a 5.1kW installation, including inspections and permits. The federal residential clean energy tax credit ended for setups completed after December 31, 2025, but some state and local incentives may still apply.

You're spending a small fortune on solar panels, but the good part is that they usually lose output over time rather than suddenly dying on you after a few years. That's why taking a long and hard look at performance warranties could sometimes be just as important as looking at the upfront cost.

If the cost of a permanent rooftop array seems too much and backup power is your main goal, you can get a portable power station instead. Brands like Anker SOLIX, Jackery, BLUETTI and EcoFlow sell units that can charge up from a single panel or several compatible solar panels to keep a limited number of appliances powered on during a power outage.
