#296. NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain

“We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”

SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

For SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

The Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.

Other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.

Ars recently spoke with Steve Creech, the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.

For Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a New Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.

Then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.

NASA changed the plan for the Artemis III mission earlier this year, rerouting the flight plan from a lunar mission to a low-Earth orbit mission. This means the Artemis program’s first crewed lunar landing will be on Artemis IV, targeted to launch before the end of 2028.

So, why is Artemis III seemingly testing so much more with Blue Origin than with Starship? Creech told Ars that a big reason is to maintain SpaceX’s focus on orbital refueling. Blue Origin no longer requires in-space refueling for Artemis landing missions. Also, SpaceX has extensive experience with life support systems with its Dragon crewed spacecraft. Blue Origin has comparatively little.

“The bigger challenges for [SpaceX] were the prop transfer and getting to the uncrewed landing demo,” Creech said. “The thing that we’re going to learn more with Starship is, when we dock with Orion, they will have control of the attitude, control of the stack. That integrated stack control will be on the Starship side. So, with that huge of a vehicle, I think we’re going to learn more on that.

“With Blue, we’re going to have Orion control the stack for this mission,” Creech said. “When we get to a later mission, the Blue lander with fully loaded prop will have to control the stack. But with Blue, trying to mitigate risk, we’re going to have Orion do that.”

Artemis III will be Blue Origin’s first time flying a crew cabin for orbital spaceflight. Blue Origin has experience with suborbital space tourism, but those flights were brief and didn’t require the level of advanced life support necessary for longer durations. Blue Origin and NASA will emphasize those test objectives on Artemis III.

“I think SpaceX’s part was really, we need to focus on the docking,” Creech said. “If we added a crew cabin, that would slow us down on the other things and not add to what we’re already doing.”

The Starship on Artemis III will have a full complement of Raptor engines and a docking port on its nose. Blue Moon will not have any main engines when it links up with Orion on Artemis III, only a set of smaller thrusters for pointing control and minor maneuvers.

“With Blue, you don’t have a BE-7 engine, you don’t have the cryo tanks,” Creech said. “They’re representing the mass of the lander when it comes back from the surface because we think that’s the most critical case. But it does have the crew cabin.”

While there’s no Starship life support demonstration on Artemis III, NASA added a new milestone to SpaceX’s Moon lander contract to test parts of its crew cabin on the ground. The additional testing involves construction of a prototype crew compartment, called Cabin One, at SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, Texas.

NASA levied new test requirements on Blue Origin, too. The company plans to launch its first Blue Moon test mission early next year after a monthslong delay caused by a rocket explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in May. This version of Blue Moon, known as Mark 1, has a single hydrogen-fueled BE-7 main engine. Future human-rated landers from Blue Origin will have three.

“One of the things we added into the program in the last year is, we really felt like we needed a test of the three-engine configuration,” Creech said. The hotfire test of the three-engine Blue Moon propulsion unit will occur inside a vacuum chamber at NASA’s In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio.

This year’s Artemis shakeup did more than change the flight plan for Artemis III. Engineers also altered the architecture for subsequent lunar landing missions. The updated plans will make life easier for teams working on Starship and Blue Moon. That’s not necessarily the case for Orion.

“Our previous architecture for both these landers required a 90-day loiter in lunar orbit for Orion to arrive,” Creech said. “That was something that, for both of these landers, drove a lot of complexity, and a lot of it made the lander job really hard.”

The new concept of operations removes some of that complexity, according to NASA.

“One of the things we changed was that 90-day loiter,” Creech said. “SpaceX, they solved it by saying let’s do an Earth orbit rendezvous with Orion, and take Orion to the Moon. For both Blue Origin and SpaceX, we have updated their requirements to a four-day surface day initially. Before, our initial missions were six-and-a-half days.”

The six-and-a-half-day surface stay was baked into the Artemis architecture because the Orion spacecraft was originally planned to settle into a long, looping path around the Moon, called a near-rectilinear halo orbit. This orbit was predicated by the expected location of NASA’s now-canceled Gateway lunar space station. That, in turn, was driven by Orion’s inability to reach an orbit closer to the Moon.

Now, instead of rendezvousing with Starship near the Moon on landing missions, Orion will link up with Starship in high-Earth orbit. From there, Starship will propel it toward the Moon.

What’s still unclear, however, is whether SpaceX will have to refuel Starship at an altitude above low-Earth orbit. A graphic presented by Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, last month illustrated this possibility with a “final tanking orbit” before Starship docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit.

“We’re still working that out,” Creech said. “We’re making progress, but where we actually rendezvous with Orion is still in trade, so that’s why you saw a little bit of fuzziness there.”

For missions using Blue Moon, the lander will connect with Orion in orbit around the Moon. Blue Origin’s updated plans do away with the requirement for in-space refueling but will still require four launches of the company’s New Glenn rocket, one for the Blue Moon lander itself and three with transfer stages to boost it out of Earth orbit to the Moon.

A new stretched Centaur upper stage for the Space Launch System should give the rocket energy to send Orion to low-lunar orbit, which it could not reach with the current version of SLS. NASA has not determined if the new Centaur exploration stage will be ready in time for Artemis IV. If not, Artemis IV could fly with the last of NASA’s in-stock SLS upper stages.

NASA is also waiting to decide which lander to use on Artemis IV. In either case, two of Orion’s four astronauts will transfer into the landers for the final descent to the lunar surface for a four-day stay, then take off and return to Orion.

Starship and Blue Moon must each complete an uncrewed landing demonstration before a crewed lunar mission. The landing demos are targeted for late 2027 or early 2028, Creech said, but they won’t necessarily test everything crews will need when they head for the lunar south pole.

Starship’s elevator, for example, is not part of SpaceX’s uncrewed landing demonstration. Engineers will use a test lab at Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama to check the elevator’s performance in a simulated lunar environment.

NASA did not initially require SpaceX or Blue Origin to prove their landers could take off from the Moon before a crew mission. Government officials later added the lunar takeoff requirement for each company’s uncrewed landing demos.

For now, NASA is leaving the details of the uncrewed takeoff demo up to SpaceX and Blue Origin. During Apollo, NASA’s lunar lander never landed on the Moon before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin descended to the Sea of Tranquility. NASA did, however, fly a dress rehearsal around the Moon on Apollo 10 that included a test of the lunar module’s landing abort capability.

“Where we are today is, Blue will land and then do a full ascent back to the rendezvous point with Orion,” Creech said. “With SpaceX. They will land, they will take off again, get to main stage on the engines, and then they will do another landing on the surface.”

That could change. Today’s plan gives SpaceX two shots at proving Starship can safely land on the Moon, but it comes with trade-offs.

“When I came into the program, I was like, ‘Why are we not going all the way to the rendezvous point?’” said Creech, who took over as HLS program manager in 2025. “Some of my key people felt strongly we would get more out of the way we’re doing it now. There are others that have different opinions… We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”

For Starship, orbital refueling remains the key to the Moon. SpaceX’s propellant transfer demonstration will involve two Starships, one launched from Florida and another from Texas, docking together in low-Earth orbit and transferring a “meaningful” amount of propellant from one ship to the other, Creech said.

“The first quarter of next year, we will see a long-awaited propellant transfer test from SpaceX, where they launch two Starships in pretty close proximity, actually dock, and transfer, we’re calling it a meaningful amount, of propellant,” Creech told Ars. “That is going to be a big learning point if they pull that off, because their architecture depends on propellant aggregation and multiple propellant flights.”

The propellant transfer test will mark the first time one spacecraft has offloaded a significant quantity of cryogenic propellants—in this case, methane and liquid oxygen—onto another vehicle in space. It is the culmination of decades of government and commercial research on cryogenic orbital refueling. The results will tell engineers how much of the propellant will be lost from boil-off during the transfer.

That is one reason why there’s still so much ambiguity about how many Starship refueling tankers SpaceX will need to launch to give the Starship lunar lander enough gas to fly to the Moon. Without refueling, Starships are restricted to flights in low-Earth orbit.

The low end of the estimate for Starship tankers is six to eight refueling flights to support a Starship lunar mission. Those numbers come from Elon Musk, SpaceX’s founder and CEO, and fall below NASA’s own conservative planning figure of 20 refueling launches. Musk’s figures hinge on future Starship upgrades to reach the vehicle’s full potential. SpaceX’s goal is to get Starship’s lift capacity up to 100 to 200 metric tons of payload to low-Earth orbit. Today’s version of Starship, known as Starship V3, is still far short of 100 metric tons of payload capacity.

For context, a Starship carries 1,600 metric tons of propellant with its tanks full. Refueling flights using future, fully optimized Starships might be able to fill those tanks with as few as six tankers. That is not the case today.

SpaceX is working on a taller, heavier Starship called Starship V4. It will fly with nine Raptor engines, an upgrade over the six-engine variant flying today. In 2025, Musk said Starship V4’s first launch was targeted for 2027. There hasn’t been a recent update to the schedule for Starship V4.

The initial Artemis lunar missions will use Starship V3, Creech said.

#295. The cool phone camera trick that can test your remote control's battery

Your phone camera is useful for more than just food pics.

Smartphones are capable of many impressive and useful feats, from capturing detailed images of objects as far away as the moon to serving as a key part of our home security systems. But smartphones are also useful for much more mundane tasks, such as helping us figure out whether our TV remote's batteries are dead.

When you press a button on your remote control, it sends that command to your TV using infrared light. While many modern televisions ship with Bluetooth remotes that support features like voice control, they may still rely on an infrared emitter for basic functions like turning the TV on or off. The emitter is located at the front of the remote. It's a tiny LED on the front of the remote that's usually easy to spot, although some modern remotes hide it behind a dark plastic window.

To test your battery, launch your phone's Camera app, point it at the front of your remote and press and hold a button while looking at your phone's screen. The remote's power button is probably best, since many Bluetooth remotes still use infrared for that command. If you see a flashing light, usually slightly purple, on the front of your remote, it means the batteries still have enough power.

The camera trick also helps you check whether your remote control uses infrared or Bluetooth for other buttons. If you press, say, the volume control and don't see a flashing light, then that command uses Bluetooth. Now, while this is a pretty cool trick, it can't diagnose every remote control problem. For example, a damaged button might not register your presses at all, so you might not see the infrared emitter flash even if your remote's batteries are working perfectly fine.

If you don't want to deal with remote control issues, you may be able to use your phone instead. Certain Android phones have built-in IR blasters; if yours does, you can set it up as a virtual remote control for your TV using an IR remote app. Modern smart TV operating systems like Android TV and Fire OS also let you use your smartphone as a remote control, even if it doesn't feature an IR emitter. You'll need to install a companion app on your phone, log in to the same account as your TV and connect both devices to the same Wi-Fi network.

For example, the Google Home app works with smart TVs powered by Google TV and Android TV. You can navigate the user interface using D-pad controls, adjust the volume or search for movie titles faster using your phone's keyboard. If the virtual remote won't turn your TV on, you may need to configure your TV's network standby settings. Some models call this feature Wake-on-LAN. Once enabled, you'll never need to worry about dead batteries in your remote control again.

#294. Why your monitor flickers when you turn it on and can it be fixed?

Your screen might be telling you something.

If you're someone who spends a decent amount of time in front of a computer, perhaps at work or during long gaming sessions, you may have noticed just how finicky certain parts of your computer can be. That's especially true of its peripherals and accessories, with one of the usual suspects being your monitor.

Turning on your monitor and noticing some unusual oddities, specifically flickering, may seem like an apocalyptic beginning to your day. Monitors of decent quality are pretty affordable today, but no one wants to spend money on a new display if they don't have to. Thankfully, your computer monitor is fairly easy to troubleshoot on a basic level in order to determine your ideal path forward.

If it's something more difficult to solve — something deeper at a hardware level — that can become a bit harder to resolve on your own. Taking some simple steps to determine the cause and potential fixes can save you a lot of headaches in the long run.

A monitor starting to flicker could stem from a rather wide variety of different issues. One of the most common reasons for a flickering monitor is a loose or potentially faulty display cable, whether that's a modern HDMI or DisplayPort cable, or even an older VGA one. Reinserting the cables or checking them for damage or fraying can be a quick fix.

If you are suspicious that the cable is defective, you could also try swapping the cable out for a new one. If it's not the cable, it may potentially be a bad port on the monitor or the PC itself, which would necessitate trying a different port on the monitor or computer if they have more than one. If you're uncertain which one may potentially be causing the problem, you could also try hooking the monitor up to a different computer that you know with absolute certainty works. If it works without issue, you know who the culprit is.

Barring a connection issue of some kind, a flickering monitor can also be caused by something at a software level. The first things to look into are your graphics drivers. Out-of-date graphics drivers are one of the most common causes of display issues, and a simple update to them may be just what you need. On the other hand, a graphics driver update does have the potential to actually cause display problems, so rolling back to a previous version could also work.

You may also be running into an issue with the monitor's refresh rate. For example, if your monitor runs at 120Hz but your Windows 11 PC's refresh rate is set to something entirely different, it can cause some havoc. In order to fix this, all you need to do is go to Settings, then find System on the left panel, then look for Display. Look for Advanced display, then change the refresh rate to match your monitor.

If you find that your flickering monitor can't be fixed by any normal means, it may be time to look at the issues a little deeper. A consistent, almost shuttering flicker is a surefire sign that the monitor is about to crash and burn. That's especially true when you're unable to solve the issue at a hardware or software level.

The monitor may also experience blackouts, as in sudden hard cuts to black, before returning to normal operation. Your display is quite keen about letting you know when something has gone haywire, and you can do a lot of diagnosing by just examining how your display is behaving.

Faded, dim colors or vertical lines that are swimming through the screen are also a couple of telltale signs. If you think of your monitor like you would a TV and utilize similar modalities, you'll be able to diagnose it in a similar way. If you've already exhausted all your other options but still find that your display looks unhealthy, then it most likely is.

At this point, your options really narrow themselves down to two. You can either look for someone to repair the monitor or seek out a replacement. Whether you should replace or repair the monitor ultimately depends on your budget, but the price of new OLED and 4K screens is starting to tumble. In most cases, it may be better to sell it for parts or donate it and just buy something new.

#293. Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded

A recent brightening turned out to be from a star orbiting inside another.

In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.

In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it’s really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”

Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.

Karambelkar’s team spotted a candidate system where this might be happening while searching Andromeda for stars changing in brightness, using the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) telescope at Palomar Observatory and data from NASA’s Near-Earth Object Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (NEOWISE) mission. One giant had been brightening for seven years. “When a star first swallows its companion, it has a very subtle effect on its brightness,” Karambelkar said. “It slowly brightens, and a lot of light comes out in the infrared.”

In April 2025, Karambelkar’s team published a paper suggesting that this system, named AT 2025abao, was undergoing an engulfment in progress. Back then, though, they couldn’t rule out a competing explanation: a single star with instabilities deep within its core. So, they kept watching.

The researchers reconstructed the history of the system using observations from about a dozen telescopes and surveys, going back to photographic sky plates from 1989. Until 2018, the star barely changed. Modeling those quiet years revealed a giant late in its life, about 350 times wider than the Sun. Its companion was impossible to see, however. “The giant star outshines the smaller star by a factor of about 18,000,” Karambelkar said.

To get around it, the team estimated the mass of the smaller companion based on the amount of dust the system had shed before the engulfment. The estimates suggested a star of roughly 0.7 solar masses.

Between 2018 and early 2025, the giant brightened two- to threefold in visible light, swelling while its temperature stayed nearly constant. Karambelkar compares the process to a spacecraft reentering Earth’s atmosphere. The companion, skimming through the giant’s outer layers, was gradually seeing its orbit shrink, and the friction was heating up the envelope. The energy released by that drag matched the extra light the team observed.

Then, the star’s visible light dropped by half while its infrared glow kept rising. NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope happened to catch it in July 2025, revealing that the giant had swollen to some 860 times the Sun’s width and wrapped itself in fresh dust.

In October 2025, the star brightened roughly 100-fold in just 25 days, shining like 1.5 million Suns at its peak. “At one point, the rate at which the orbit was decaying became very, very fast,” Karambelkar said, comparing the release of the gravitational energy to an explosion. “The companion just fell very quickly, very deep inside the envelope of the star, and it crashed into the core. That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star, and that explosion caused it to brighten very quickly and eject some of the material.”

The eruption had all the hallmarks of a luminous red nova, a type of outburst known to come from merging stars—but an event the researchers weren’t expecting. “Honestly, our minds were blown,” Karambelkar said. He said that this was evidence that this explosion was a consequence of the inspiraling of a binary companion. What made AT 2025abao special, though, was the giant itself.

All previously known luminous red novae came from younger stars with dense, tightly bound outer layers, which inevitably drive both stars toward a merger. This one was an old giant with a loose, churning envelope—the setup that can also leave behind a surviving tight binary. To find out if the companion actually survived, the team looked at how AT 2025abao’s energy was spent.

To predict how such events end, astronomers use a formula with an efficiency parameter describing how much of the energy lost by the sinking companion goes into blowing the envelope away. AT 2025abao showed that the energy goes to different places at different stages.

During the slow spiral, most of the energy escaped as light. In the final plunge, the companion released about a hundred times more energy, but only around 1 percent of it was radiated away. Nearly all the rest went into hurling a tenth of the envelope outward at about 10 times the speed needed to escape the giant’s gravity. The rest of the envelope stayed put, which suggests the companion merged with the giant’s core instead of surviving as a tight partner.

“Initially, when the rate of energy deposition is low, the star is able to puff up and adjust to this new energy source inside it,” Karambelkar said. “But once the energy deposition rate increases very quickly as the companion spirals even closer, the star can no longer adjust itself. At that point, it needs to throw out some of its material.”

The efficiency the team calculated fits values inferred from known post-engulfment binaries. But the formula assumes the energy is mostly spent expelling lots of the envelope. Here, most of it went into flinging a small amount of gas at high speeds. It turned out the formula works as a rule of thumb but misses some of the physics.

In AT 2025abao, gas shed during the slow spiral piled up in the plane of the binary’s orbit, so the explosion’s ejecta could expand freely toward the poles even though it was blocked around the equator. That, Karambelkar argues, explains the hourglass-shaped nebulae seen around dying stars. “It had been an idea for a very long time that those hourglass shapes are shaped by binary interactions,” he said. “It seems like what we’re seeing here confirms that hypothesis.”

The team admits it can’t yet be sure the stars merged, because dust formed from the ejected material hides whatever is left inside. “We want to continue monitoring the system for several years, possibly even decades, to watch the dust clear out and whatever is remaining inside emerge,” Karambelkar said. “That will conclusively tell us whether this merged or the binary system survived.” In the meantime, the team hopes to find many more such events involving stars of different masses and types.

Telescopes we have today can detect them only as far as Andromeda, but the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should spot them in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within some 50 million light-years. “We can have an influx of several of these events per year,” Karambelkar said.

Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z

#292. Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation

Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with  her colleagues focused largely on science:  "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."

#291. How to safely clean your PC's GPU to avoid damaging it in the process

Removing and cleaning a GPU can be intimidating, but it's actually pretty simple.

Like any PC component, your graphics processing unit collects dust over time. In turn, that can affect its thermal performance, causing your card to run at lower clock speeds and, over time, shorten its lifespan. With GPU prices what they are in 2026, you don't want to replace your current one if you can avoid it. So it's a good idea to clean your GPU every three to six months or so.

Opening your case and removing the GPU to clean it can be intimidating, but if you follow this guide, you'll learn how to do it safely.

When I go to clean my PC's GPU, I find it's best to remove it from the case. This ensures any dust is cleared entirely from the system.

Safely removing the GPU starts with properly powering down your PC, and then opening the case to access the internal components. Depending on the design of your case, you may not need a screwdriver to crack open your chassis; some configurations only require loosening some thumbscrews. With older cases, you might need a Phillips head screwdriver. If you don't own one already, iFixit sells a handful of great bit kits for DIY repairs. As an additional precaution, spending about $8 on an anti-static wrist strap is also worthwhile, but not necessary.

Once you have all the tools you need in front of you, start by turning off your PC and unplugging any cables that are connected to it. Next, switch the power supply unit to the "O" position, and then press and hold down your PC's power button for about 30 seconds to discharge all the capacitors inside. Your computer is now safe to open. If you bought an anti-static wrist strap, now is the time to put it on and attach the ground to your PC's case.

With your PC powered down, you can now safely remove the GPU. I find this is easiest to do if I lay the case horizontally on a table. If you still have the box your video card came in, dig it out and get the anti-static bag ready. (You didn't throw that out, did you?) Next, follow the steps below in the exact order listed. If at any point you encounter resistance, do not try to force your GPU out of its PCIe slot.

Once you've safely removed your video card from your PC, you can now go about cleaning it. For this part of the process, you'll need an air blower or a can of compressed air. I prefer the former as it's a one-time purchase. A microfiber cloth and 90 percent isopropyl alcohol are also handy if your GPU requires a deeper clean.

It's fine if you don't feel comfortable removing your GPU; you can still clean it following the advice laid out below. However, ideally take your PC somewhere outside and dust it there.

If you take nothing else from this guide, remember this next tip. When you go to clean the fans, use a hand to keep them in place, and then use a duster or compressed air to dislodge any debris. Do not allow the fans to spin freely when you blow air into them. This can over-spin a fan, damaging its bearings and sending current back into the card's fan controller. If you're using compressed air, keep the can upright to prevent it from spraying liquid propellant.

If your GPU's backplate and protective casing are dusty, apply some isopropyl alcohol to a clean microfiber cloth and gently wipe down those parts, being careful that the cloth does not get caught on any solder joints. With your GPU out of the case, this is also a great opportunity to clean other components.

Once your GPU is clean, reinsert it following the steps above in reverse order. Two things worth flagging: First, insert your GPU into your PC's fastest PCIe slot. On most motherboards, that's the top-most slot. Second, when you go to re-plug the PCIe power cables, make sure they're properly seated.

With regular cleaning, your current GPU should last you for years to come. If you find it collects a lot of dust in between cleanings, you may want to rethink your PC's cooling setup. In my experience, a case with slightly positive air pressure is best for reducing the frequency of your PC-component cleanings. Put another way, you want your PC to intake more air than it expels. This makes it more likely for air to travel through your PC's dust filters. It's a setup that's not possible with every case, so don't sweat it if it's not perfectly achievable with your computer.

Conversely, if you're not happy with your GPU's thermals even after cleaning it, it's worth playing with the fan curve of your case fans, and configuring them to speed up with the temperature of your video card. How you go about this will depend on your build, so I can't provide specific instructions. Apps like Fan Control can help you get started. As a rule of thumb, if your GPU runs anywhere between 60 degrees to 80 degrees Celsius under full load, it's in a good place. Obviously, cooler is better, but there are a lot of factors that can affect GPU thermals.

Lastly, if you've owned your current GPU for a while, repasting it may be worthwhile. Precisely how to go about that is outside the scope of this guide, but you can find plenty of tutorials on YouTube.

#290. This free app connects your Android phone to your Windows PC wirelessly

No subscriptions, accounts or extra programs taking up space on your PC.

Moving files between an Android phone and a Windows PC is broadly a solved problem. You can use a cloud service like Google Drive as an intermediary, although uploading from one device and downloading on the other can be time-consuming. Connecting via USB is also an option, though you lose the convenience of a wireless connection. Quick Share on Android offers a good middle ground, letting you transfer files directly.

None of these help if you need to do more than move files around, though. For that, you'll need third-party programs that offer more features, like a media browser and phone mirroring. The downside is that they often require installing software on both devices and often charge a subscription fee. PlainApp, though, is different: it's a free, open-source program that lets you view and manage your Android phone's files on your computer — without installing any additional software on your PC. It also doesn't ask you to create an account or log in.

PlainApp is available on the Play Store and supports phones running Android 9 or newer. To use it, install the app, grant it notification and file access permissions and note the URL it displays. As long as your computer is connected to the same Wi-Fi network as your Android phone, you can access your phone's files wirelessly through any web browser at that URL.

PlainApp uses a self-signed TLS certificate, so your browser will show a warning the first time you access the URL. Click on Advanced > Proceed to bypass this warning. Finally, click Log in and tap Allow on your phone when prompted. Once connected, you can view and manage images, videos, music and contacts stored on your Android phone straight from your computer's browser.

The web app's user interface is simple but modern enough to feel like a polished application rather than a basic file transfer utility. The Files tab lets you browse all accessible folders and files, as well as transfer files both ways. You can send text to your phone's clipboard, call a number directly from the web GUI and use a screen-mirroring feature that shows your phone's screen in your computer's browser. PlainApp says that remote control is possible here — much like iPhone Mirroring on macOS — but I couldn't get it to work on my phone.

PlainApp's media viewer handles images and videos and shows them in original quality. If your browser does not support HEVC video playback, PlainApp will automatically convert the video to H.264. You can also use the built-in image editor, which offers basic tools for cropping, adding text or drawing directly on your photos. There's also a music player if audio's more your thing. Overall, while Quick Share is still faster for transferring photos or videos, PlainApp is much more versatile if you want to browse and organize more of your phone's contents wirelessly.

#289. Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private.

Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router to another one. Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

#288. Can you safely use a 140w charger on an iPhone?

The simple answer is yes, an iPhone can tolerate a 140-watt charger, but it's not a simple process, and there are safety considerations. A 140-watt charger is an upper limit that your iPhone will never reach because even the latest iPhone 18 Pro hits its cap at 52W. An iPhone can only pull what it can pull, and it's nowhere near 140W. USB PD used to top out at 100W, but the newer range is between 100W and 240W, now known as Extended Power Range (EPR). EPR adds 28V, 36V and 48V options. Once a device is in EPR mode, it has to send a "keep-alive" message every half second. If the charger doesn't receive that message, it drops back down to 5V. An iPhone's requirements are well below that threshold.

Potential safety issues are generally on the charger's end. Apple is pretty blunt about using third-party chargers that fail to meet safety standards, claiming it could cause injury and even death. Obviously, that's something iPhone users should avoid, so stick with reputable brands. Yes, Apple's own power adapters and cables are priced like they have 24k gold in them, but there are plenty of options out there that meet safety standards and cost much less.

Far less than 140W. The iPhone 17, 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max reach 50 percent in about 20 minutes with a 40W or higher adapter. The iPhone Air and iPhone 17e only need 20W to hit 50 percent in roughly half an hour. For an iPhone 15 or 16 (or an older Lightning model like the iPhone 14 with a USB-C to Lightning cable), a USB PD adapter 18W or greater is needed for fast charging. The iPhone 18 Pro series and the iPhone Duo step things up a bit. The best and fastest charger for these phones is a 60W adapter with Adjustable Voltage Supply (AVS) and USB PD 3.2, plus a USB-C cable that can handle 60W or more.

None of that approaches 140W. The best use case for 140W+ is a high-performance laptop or charging several devices at the same time. If you have an Apple adapter (Apple doesn't supply them with iPhones/iPads for environmental purposes), the wattage is printed on the top or bottom. Apple prints the Dynamic Power Symbol on their 40W chargers. You can also get a fairly accurate estimate of charging time directly from your iPhone. On iOS 18 or later, a Slow Charger message appears on the Lock Screen and under Settings > Battery. iOS 26 ramps up the convenience by alerting you when you're using an incompatible charger that isn't charging your iPhone.

Not much, unless it's a USB-C port with Power Delivery. At base specs, USB 2.0 ports supply 5V at 500mA or 2.5W. USB 3.0 and 3.1 ports bump it up to 900mA or 4.5W. The Battery Charging 1.2 spec ports can reach 1.5A or 7.5W. If you prefer to charge from a PC or laptop, it's a bit chaotic. For instance, orange ports on Intel NUC PCs are rated at 1.5A, and the blue ones are 900 milliamps. Black ports are typically USB 2.0 and have a modest 2.5W default. Those examples sound pretty sluggish because they are. Plug an iPhone 18 Pro Max into a USB 2.0, and it's gonna be a while. The iPhone 15 and later are capped at 7.5W on a USB-A charger. Fortunately, USB-C is a major upgrade over USB-A, with 15W (5V at 3A) without Power Delivery.

With Power Delivery, it skyrockets to 100W in the Standard Power Range and 240W with EPR. On top of that, standard USB-C cables are rated for 3A, hitting their ceiling at 60W, while 100W feature e-marked 5A cables. These cables have a tiny chip that tells the charger what it can handle. EPR cables encompass everything above 100W. A "typical USB port" is ultimately defined by the individual. For someone who uses a fairly standard 20W adapter for an iPhone, a USB-A port may be considered typical, but a specialized USB-A charger can push up to 18W. In other words, what is "typical" depends on what you're using and what you're used to.

#287. Germany's religious freedom report: Authoritarian regimes, holy wars, and spies abroad

Harassment, persecution, surveillance: Across much of the world, people of faith are facing growing pressure. A new German government report is unusually direct in criticizing China in particular.

The report spans more than 150 pages, but its conclusion can be summed up in a single sentence: "The global situation regarding freedom of religion and belief deteriorated during the reporting period," said Thomas Rachel, the German government's commissioner for freedom of religion and belief, and a member of parliament for the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Recently adopted by the Cabinet, the government's fourth report on the subject covers developments from 2023 to 2025.

The government has issued a dedicated report on freedom of religion and belief around the world. According to the report, this freedom is facing "increasing pressure" globally. The focus is not primarily on the suppression of religious institutions or structures, but on the situation of individuals who hold a religious belief, or none at all.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The importance of religious freedom is reflected in the way the government commissioner describes the issue: "Religion and faith are of great importance to four out of five people around the world and are central to their identity. People wake up with God and go to sleep with God. It is part of their everyday lives." Research by the Pew Research Center suggests that about 84% of the world's population identifies with a certain religion.

At a time when authoritarian regimes are gaining ground and expanding their surveillance capabilities, the report paints a bleak picture. The growing number of violent conflicts, the rise of authoritarian rule, and the spread of populism have led to "painful restrictions on freedom of religion and belief around the world."

The German government report does not attempt to provide a statistical tally of attacks or the number of people facing persecution. Instead, it examines 30 countries as case studies where, in the federal government's view, freedom of religion and belief is being restricted. These include about six countries each from Africa, Asia, and the Arab world. In Europe, the report focuses on Belarus, Russia, Ukraine, and Turkey, while in Latin America it highlights Mexico, Nicaragua, and Cuba. It also identifies shortcomings in five of the world's six most populous countries: China, India, Indonesia, Pakistan, and Nigeria.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regarding India, the report refers to "Hindu nationalist efforts" that threaten the equal treatment of all officially recognized religions. It states that the generally peaceful coexistence of different faiths is "repeatedly overshadowed by tensions and, at times, violence." Both Muslim and Christian communities report growing intolerance and hate speech. According to the report, violent Hindu extremist groups have carried out a "large number of physical attacks" against Muslims, while the police and government authorities often respond inadequately.

In China, the German government identifies a "significant tightening of the legal framework of state control at the expense of freedom of religion and belief." According to the report, this particularly affects Uyghurs, Tibetans and churches that lack official state approval and are subject to harsh measures by the authorities. The law on the "Promotion of Ethnic Unity and Progress," which came into force on July 1, 2026, subordinates religion to "the formation of national identity" and patriotic education.

One of the countries where the situation has deteriorated most dramatically is Nicaragua, which has severely restricted freedom of religion and belief since 2018. The repression has primarily targeted the Catholic Church. According to the report, "intimidation, persecution, imprisonment, and expulsion" have forced around 130 priests and nuns to leave the country.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The reports reserves some of its sharpest criticism for Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox Church. Under his leadership, the church has strongly supported Russia's war against Ukraine and portrayed it as a "holy war." According to the report, "weapons are blessed, Russian soldiers are absolved of their sins, and donations are collected for the war." It is perhaps the clearest example in the report of how religion can be used to justify oppression and violence.

The report explicitly addresses the threat posed by "transnational repression" (TNR), which it describes as a "growing global problem" that also affects Germany. The term refers to the persecution or intimidation of individuals by their country of origin beyond its own borders.

Ultimately, it argues, this amounts to a "continuation of domestic repression." Such "cross-border repression" has become considerably easier through the growing availability of digital means of repression, including smear campaigns on social media and spyware.

These forms of pressure range from physical attacks on individuals to digital assaults such as online intimidation and defamation. In some cases, repression is also carried out by threatening family members who remain in the country of origin. Russia and Iran, for example, are identified as the "main perpetrators of transnational repression" in Germany.

China is a particularly prominent example of religious and ideological tensions. Repression by Beijing in Germany primarily targets members of groups that the country's Communist Party classifies as "hostile to the system." These include Uyghurs, Tibetans, and members of the Falun Gong movement. According to the report, they are "also subject to surveillance and repressive measures in Germany," while relatives living in China are pressured.

Thomas Rachel hopes the newly published report will be "discussed in as many Bundestag committees as possible" and that members of parliament will "engage with the issue accordingly." Previous government reports on the subject have been debated in the Bundestag plenary at least once and, in some cases, twice.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The issue's place within the German government has also changed during the current legislative term. Commissioner Thomas Rachel is now based at the Foreign Ministry, while both of his predecessors since 2018 were attached to the Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development. Today, Rachel says, the importance of religion is being "taken into account" in German foreign policy. He also points to his involvement in the Foreign Ministry's diplomatic training programs.

In doing so, the government led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) reversed a structural decision made by the previous center-left coalition, which was led from 2021 to 2025 by Chancellor Olaf Scholz of the Social Democratic Party (SPD). The Scholz government had reduced the issue's prominence by assigning it to the "Religion and Foreign Policy" division. Religion and foreign policy have now regained a more prominent place within government.

One example is the current foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, who has already visited the Vatican more often than his two predecessors combined. In addition, alongside Rachel, the ministry has for some time maintained a dedicated unit headed by an ambassador that deals with, among other things, "fundamental issues relating to religion and foreign policy."

#286. Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

Meta is “re-evaluating” 2030 sustainability goals. Will others follow?

Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

That would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and New Hampshire. The company attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

For comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

Meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”

It would very much be in the public interest for other Big Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#284. The pros and cons of sharing your location

Some apps really do need to know where you are, but plenty of others don't.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When you download an app on a smartphone, you're usually prompted to agree to a list of permissions it needs to function. You may be asked to share your device's location when the app is open or grant unrestricted access in the background. Even website pop-ups halt your scrolling to ask for your location.

It can be difficult to pick between staying in the dark and trading your location for services like maps, food deliveries and device tracking. Outside of those use cases, you may want to share your location from your iPhone with a friend or family member.

Today's devices have more safety features than they used to. Google, for instance, reviews Android apps that ask for background location access. But location data can be resold to third parties, so sharing it with apps and services you don't trust is risky. Here's how to weigh the pros and cons.

Staying connected makes your devices easier to find. While Find My is an easy smartphone anti-theft pick, sharing your location data with Apple AirTags and Tile trackers that work via Bluetooth lets you see your belongings in real time on a map. They can even play audio alerts, so you won't have to worry about losing your car keys inside your apartment again.

On a night out, people often share their location with friends for a sense of safety. Uber's Share My Trip feature lets you send your trip status and live location to up to five contacts. Snapchat's Snap Map, meanwhile, uses your location to track where you've made memories and find hotspots of activity to plan your next hangout. If you've set up the Personal Safety app on your Pixel phone, it can automatically call 911 and share your location if it detects a severe car crash.

You can also share your location for a set time on your iPhone. iOS 26 lets you share for an hour, a day or indefinitely, and iOS 27 adds a custom option that runs from 15 minutes to 30 days. iOS 27 also lets you temporarily hide your location from people you normally share it with. On Android smartphones, Google's Find My Device app lets contacts share their location with you for a set duration as well. If you're meeting someone, you can also share your real-time location in Google Maps with an estimated time of arrival.

Sometimes you have no choice but to share your location data. Getting directions from Google Maps or Apple Maps, whether in a new city or on your home turf, requires letting the app see where you are. As a parent, you may want to see your children's location via services like Google Family Link. As a partner, maybe you shouldn't, even though many couples do. A Life360 survey of 1,000 US adults in relationships found that 95 percent use some form of location-sharing tech.

This can take a turn for the worse when personal safety is involved. Fitness-tracking apps like Strava store information on your jogging routines, revealing patterns that a stalker may use to deliberately run into you if you leave your information public. This goes for geotagged social media posts as well. Adding your location to a public Instagram Story might help your friends find you, but live updates like these may also draw attention from strangers.

In some cases, you may be able to get away with giving your location data momentarily or refusing altogether. Try not to hand out your location data to services that don't really need it to function. Delivery apps work just fine with manually entered addresses instead of being allowed to track your location. You can also use their browser-based versions to reduce the information you share.

#281. How to use AI glasses as a teleprompter

If you have the right type of smart glasses, this is an easy feature to enable.

Out of all the myriad variations of smart glasses available today, the ones with built-in waveguides — such as the XGIMI MemoMind One and Even Realities G2 — have the most utility. Having a screen projected in your field of view that shows notifications, turn-by-turn directions or real-time translations is particularly useful outdoors. The best part about using the MemoMind One and Even G2 is that these smart glasses don't have a camera, so there's no social stigma to using them outside.

These glasses also have a built-in teleprompter mode that lets you deliver presentations or speeches while maintaining eye contact, and honestly, they're pretty good at it. As the waveguides project the screen in your field-of-view, it feels natural to use glasses as a teleprompter. I tested the MemoMind One and Even Realities G2 with this mode, and here's what you need to know.

The MemoMind One and Even G2 have a teleprompter feature that's easy to use; just load the script into the app, and you can select how fast (or slow) to scroll the text. Even's G2 reads PDF, plaintext, and DOCX files, but MemoMind One has just TXT and DOCX, with no PDF integration. This is mildly annoying if you regularly deal with PDF documents, but at least converting documents between file formats is trivial these days.

That said, MemoMind One has greater control over how you can view and control the teleprompter text. You can easily adjust font size, line width (which is a nice bonus), and adjust the display scaling just for the teleprompter. Both smart glasses have a nifty auto-follow feature that slows down or speeds up the text based on your speaking cadence. The feature (ostensibly) relies on AI to listen to your speech and adjusts the flow of the text accordingly. Other than that, you can get an auto-scroll option set to words per minute, and there's manual control as well.

Using the MemoMind One and Even G2 as a teleprompter is easy. I loaded up my Find X10 Pro Max review script and started talking, and the MicroLED-based waveguides did a good job projecting the text without otherwise inhibiting my field-of-view. You get to see the time elapsed (which is useful for me), along with battery level of the glasses and the current time. I don't routinely use a teleprompter, but having smart glasses to do so is far less of a hassle than setting up a dedicated one (at least in my use case).

The waveguide prisms aren't that noticeable externally (unless someone is standing within 15cm of you), so if you're in a public setting, the text won't be visible to anyone in your vicinity. If anything, smart glasses are a good option in a public speaking setting as it gives you greater mobility — your teleprompter moves with you. Also, both the MemoMind One and Even G2 have monochrome waveguides with good brightness levels, and I didn't see any issues making out the text while outdoors. I found the MemoMind One to get brighter than the G2 in outdoor use.

I've been using the Even G2 and MemoMind One interchangeably for most of the last six months. The G2 is a decent update to the G1, and I like that the case has an integrated charger — that's one less cable for me to store. MemoMind doesn't do that, so I need to store the tiny dongle carefully so I don't lose the only way to charge the glasses.

Both glasses are lightweight at under 50g, and while the Even G2 is lighter, I found the MemoMind One to be more comfortable to wear. Battery life is better on the MemoMind One, and the glasses have onboard audio and sound tuned by Harman; they're great to listen to podcasts on the go. The G2 misses out on speakers altogether, so you don't get any built-in sound.

Where the MemoMind One truly wins out is the control mechanism. The Even G2 uses a series of taps and swipe actions to control the glasses, with the gesture surface located at the temple tips, which is just awkward to use. There's also the small fact that it doesn't register gestures correctly at times, so I'm often scrolling or trying to trigger a gesture by reaching behind my ear, and it isn't the best look if you're in public.

Thankfully, the MemoMind One doesn't have these shortcomings; the glasses have a physical button located below the right hinge, and it's easy to interact. A single tap lets you cycle between menus, and a long-press action is used to exit to the dashboard. The UI wasn't quite as polished at launch, but MemoMind rolled out a slare of software updates over the last three months, and the glasses are on par with the Even G2 in this area.

Out of these smart glasses, I'd get the MemoMind One if I had to pick one. The MemoMind One just feels easier to wear, you can select three frame styles (G2 is limited to two), and it costs $499, $100 less than the G2. That's if you're getting the standard model; if you use prescription lenses, you'll need to pay an additional $280 for the MemoMind One and $159 for the Even G2. Of the two, the MemoMind One has the better feature-set as it has built-in audio and brighter waveguides, and I found it easier to wear and use.
