#278. What is the best way to secure your PlayStation 5 for a flight?

GTA 6 launches in November 2026, but unfortunately, you can't pause real life. That business trip you had planned doesn't care about your other life in Vice City, so you'll have to get creative to keep playing while you're away from home. You might be asking yourself if you should just take your PlayStation 5 along with you, and frankly, nobody here is going to judge you for that. But is it even possible to carry a big, bulky gaming console with you on a plane?

The short answer is yes. The TSA allows a PS5 in both carry-on and checked bags, but it recommends carry-on for fragile electronics. The only real issue with taking Sony's console along with you is the DualSense controller, which uses a lithium ion battery and needs some special care. The console itself just needs good padding. And if dragging your system through security sounds like too much for you, there is always the option of streaming remotely.

This decision is ultimately up to you. Both the carry-on and checked-bag options present their own advantages and disadvantages. A carry-on means you'll have to, well, carry your PS5 with you the entire trip. That doesn't leave a lot of room for much else in your bag, but it also means you can keep an eye on your console at all times. Putting it in a checked bag frees up space for the flight, but with your system out of sight, you run the risk of an airport worker mishandling your luggage or losing it.

No matter your choice, packing your PS5 carefully matters. In a carry-on, make sure you wrap your console with a sweater or some other padding, and pack the cables with it. If possible, it's best to keep the carry-on under the seat in front of you to avoid all the shoving and shifting in the overhead compartments.

In a checked bag, the ideal way to pack your PS5 would be in the original box or inside a hard shell, but that isn't always realistic. As an alternative, place the console in the center of your luggage and completely surround it with soft clothes. If you have a hard plastic suitcase, that would be preferable to a soft-sided bag.

The DualSense controller has a lithium ion battery rated at 3.65 volts and 1,560 milliamp hours, which works out to about 5.7 watt hours. That is far below the 100 watt hour limit the FAA sets for lithium-ion batteries, so the controller is allowed on a plane. Still, the FAA says devices with lithium batteries should be carried in the cabin. If the controller has to be checked, it must be completely powered off and protected from damage or accidental activation. The reason is thermal runaway — a battery overheating and catching fire — which ULSE counted at an average of 2.36 incidents per week on passenger flights in 2025. In the cabin, flight crews are trained to recognize and respond to lithium battery fires.

So keep your controller with you, make sure it is turned off or completely out of juice, and wrap it in some clothes or place it in a protective shell to keep it from getting damaged. Your best option would be an official DualSense carry case, like the one that comes with the DualSense Edge.

There is a third option that allows you to keep playing from anywhere without having to carry your PS5 with you, and that is PlayStation's Remote play. This alternative allows you to stream your games online using your phone, a tablet or a laptop via your home console. Sony requires a connection of at least 5Mbps and recommends 15Mbps for a smoother picture.

For this to work, you need to keep your home console running in rest mode with "Stay Connected to the Internet" and "Enable Turning on PS5 from Network" activated. You can find these options under Settings > System > Power Saving > Features Available in Rest Mode.

The PlayStation Portal makes this easier. It's a dedicated handheld that streams the PS5 over Wi-Fi. Sony says it works on public networks too, as long as it was first set up on the home network. Players with a PlayStation Plus Premium subscription can also use it to stream select games from Sony's servers with no console running at home.

Check the airline's carry-on size and weight limits against the console's dimensions.

Back up your save data and finish any pending updates.

Shut the console down completely, unplug everything, and take out the disc.

Wrap the power cable and HDMI cable, and pack them together with the console.

Pad the console in its original box, a hard case, or soft clothes toward the center of your luggage.

Switch the controller off and keep it in the cabin with you in a padded pouch.

At the hotel, make sure the TV has a free HDMI port before settling in.

#277. SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

“Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026.”

The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

“SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

The central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has said that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

“My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”

The communications from Himes suggest that Congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the Midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

“It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

Various options are open to Congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

It seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or launches, as the company is currently providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

#275. Public vs. private IP addresses: what's the difference?

One identifies your network, the other identifies the devices using your network.

Each time you stream a video, read an article or download files online, your network interface and a server communicate with each other using unique numerical labels called IP addresses. When you acquire an internet connection, your ISP assigns a unique public IP address to your router's WAN port. The public IP address is what allows you to access the internet and the internet to find you.

All the various gadgets connected to your home home network like phones, computers and smart home hardware connect to your router via private IP addresses rather than the public address assigned to your router. Devices on private IP addresses can communicate with each other but cannot directly access the internet; they must rely on a router. Similarly, devices outside the private network cannot communicate with those using a private IP address. This is why your neighbor cannot send a print request to your home printer.

When attempting to understand public vs. private IP address, you can think of the former as your house address and the latter as apartment numbers. Each device connected to your router is assigned a unique private IP address. Knowing how to find the IP addresses of your connected devices can help streamline troubleshooting efforts in case your home network starts acting up.

The quickest way to find your public IP address is via an online IP checker tool like WhatIsMyIPAddress and ifconfig.me. You can use any device connected to your router for this process as long as it's capable of accessing a web browser. To identify private IP addresses, you can use your router's control panel to view the list of devices connected to your home network, including their private IP addresses. However, this method may not be sufficient to identify which IP address corresponds to what device as not all device manufacturers include hostnames.

In case a device's hostname doesn't show up in your router's control panel, you're not entirely out of options. For instance, on a Windows computer, you can run the "ipconfig" command to find the IPv4 address, which is the computer's private IP address. On macOS, running the "ipconfig getifaddr en0" (Wi-Fi) or "ipconfig getifaddr en1" (ethernet) commands will pull up the computer's private IP address.

On an iPhone: Settings > Wi-Fi > tap the "i" button next to Wi-Fi network you're connected to > scroll down to find the IPv4 section containing your iPhone's private IP address. Similarly, on an Android device: Settings > Network and internet > Internet > tap the network you're connected to > scroll down to find your device's private IP address.

Your public IP address identifies your network on the internet while your private IP addresses identify devices connected to your home network. Although each device in your home network has its own private IP address, your router allows them to share a single public IP address when accessing the internet. This is made possible via Network Address Translation (NAT), which is a network routing mechanism that enables the router to manage communication between devices in your private network and the internet.

While home networks are usually assigned a private IP address that follows the 192.168.X.X IP DNS range, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has also reserved the 10.X.X.X and 172.16.X.X private IP ranges for large and medium organizations, respectively.

Learning how to recognize public and private IP addresses can help you identify devices in your home network and troubleshoot connectivity issues effectively. For instance, if a device in your network has an unusual 169.254.X.X IP address, also known as Automatic Private IP, instead of the familiar 192.168.X.X IP range, you can conclude that the device did not receive the IP address from the router. In case devices in your home network do have valid private IP addresses but no access to the internet, you can then focus your investigation on the most probable cause — your router, followed by the ISP — rather than troubleshooting everything in the network chain.

#272. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#271. 8 Windows apps you should probably remove from your PC

Not every app on your PC deserves a permanent place.

Bloatware and adware aren't new, but they feel far more prevalent these days. Not only do they take up SSD space (which is more precious than ever because of soaring storage prices), but they can also consume RAM and annoy you with alerts you don't care about.

The ubiquity of these annoyances, including junk built into Windows itself, means that debloating a fresh Windows PC has become a common practice. Some apps (both preinstalled and common third-party tools), aren't actively detrimental. But, depending on how you use your PC, it may be worth upgrading them with superior — and often inexpensive or free — options. Here are several such Windows apps you should replace or remove outright.

Media Player, not to be confused with the classic Windows Media Player from prior Windows versions, is the out-of-the-box way to listen to music or watch videos on your PC. And while it does a suitable job of playing both audio and video files from a broad range of formats, it can't compete with the features you get from alternative apps like VLC.

VLC can play tons of video formats (even rare ones) without the need for additional codecs or extensions. It can also handle media file conversions quickly and easily. If you love subtitles but have a video file that lacks them, VLC can take dragged-and-dropped .srt or .vtt files from the web. The totally-free app can do so much more once you dig into it.

It's never been easier to get into content creation, which can blossom into a potentially profitable side hustle. Even if not, it's fun sharing your creativity with close friends and anyone the algorithm pushes you towards. Microsoft Clipchamp is included in Windows 11 and offers a user-friendly way to crop, cut and edit videos in up to 1080p. Unfortunately, it keeps a lot of its flashier features, like Copilot integration and 4K exporting, along with access to premium stock assets, filters and effects, behind the Microsoft 365 paywall.

As someone who edits video almost every day, it's difficult for me to recommend anything else but CapCut to amateur creators. It's approachable for beginners while also providing plenty of features that professionals will love. And as someone leery about shoehorned AI features, I find those in CapCut actually useful (some of them, anyway).

There's a subscription here too if you want to take full advantage, starting at $19.99 per month. But it's one of the few apps on this payment model that provides substantial value.

While it might sound shallow to say, uTorrent is one of the most hideous-looking modern apps. Like many programs that offer free versions, it's full of ads and foists extra junk apps on you during installation. In 2015, uTorrent received backlash after it secretly installed Epic Scale, a Litecoin miner, with every new installation. We're more than a decade removed from this, but it's the kind of cynical action that people never really forget.

There are countless replacements, with two highlights depending on what you're after. For a uTorrent-like experience without the bloat or ads, there's qBittorrent. It's got a slightly larger footprint than uTorrent, has built-in search engines, and is widely accepted on private trackers. If you prefer a slimmed-down, barebones approach, Transmission is hard to beat.

Setting up a new PC is exciting, but also comes with some frustrations. You'll probably be dismayed to see, after dropping big bucks on a new piece of tech, that you still have to contend with pre-installed software like Norton or McAfee. It's annoying to get bombarded with alerts that your trial (which you never wanted) is ending, especially since Windows Defender is more than enough for most people.

Considering how good Defender is, McAfee, Norton, and other antivirus apps don't simply provide protection from viruses. Their paid versions add other security services such as a VPN, scam detection and support for restoring your identity if it's stolen. But if you're just looking for bog-standard protection from viruses, Defender should be vigilant enough to keep your PC safe.

Does anyone actually use these? Despite their default presence in the world's most popular desktop OS, I've never once heard of anyone actually implementing the built-in news and weather apps in their regular workflow. It's almost impressive that Microsoft still supports these, which probably see less regular use than Minesweeper.

The Weather app isn't terrible, but there's nothing particularly exciting about it and it also has annoying ads to work around. Plenty of weather sites give you more data in a cleaner experience. The News app is considerably worse, cramming tons of low-quality and clickbait stories amongst more ads. You'll have far better results curating a feed with RSS, following your favorite news publications on social media or getting alerts from their dedicated apps.

While Xbox still has dedicated consoles, Microsoft's dedicated gaming brand has taken on a more nebulous definition. It's a console, but also an app and a store, with games you can stream to many other devices. If you're a gamer, the Xbox app for Windows has plenty of features and tools like Xbox mode that come close to providing a console-like experience with the power of your PC. It's constantly updated, supports cloud gaming, lets you easily connect with friends and aggregates all your games from various storefronts in one convenient place.

But if you're not a gamer, it does little more than take up resources. Even if you are a gamer, those who stick to Steam for their games can get by without the Xbox app. That's also the case for anyone who's hopped off the Game Pass bandwagon recently.

If you want a simple example of how cynical adware has gotten in recent years, just remind yourself that in the not-too-distant past, Minesweeper and Solitaire came standard with every copy of Windows and weren't bogged down with ads like they are today. You can pay for the premium edition of Microsoft Solitaire Collection for $1.49 per month, which won't break the bank, but still feels unnecessarily rent-seeking.

But with games as simple as these, there are, luckily, many free alternatives easily accessible from your web browser. Solitaire for Free and Minesweeper for Free are exactly what they're poised as: classic versions of these games with no nonsense. Minesweeper doesn't offer much customization outside of difficulty, but Solitaire has more than 30 variations, plus light customization of its cards and background.

If you want an alternative that you can play offline, Free Solitaire on Steam is tough to beat. There are tons of different game modes and variants, lots of card customization (including personalized art if you want) and zero ads.

One of the irrefutable facts of life is that "nothing beats free." Sure, there are outliers, but if I had to cite my source for this ancient adage, it would be Google Docs and the rest of Google Workspace. Google's productivity suite features everything most people need for personal documents, spreadsheets and presentations. And web links make them easy to share with whoever needs them.

It's not a one-to-one match for Microsoft Office, which is why many professionals still need the full Microsoft suite. Microsoft Office extensions like .docx and .xlsx are the corporate standard, and while Google Docs can export to these, doing so can result in some wonky formatting.

Unfortunately, accessing Microsoft Office applications requires paying at least $9.99 per month or $99.99 per year for Microsoft 365. If you prefer the feel of a dedicated app, or are leery of letting Google take over another part of your life, there are plenty of great Microsoft Office alternatives. One is OnlyOffice, which provides a comparable Office experience while also being free (with paid options for businesses and developers).

No matter which option you choose, you can uninstall the free Microsoft Office trials that come with Windows and only serve to push you into signing up for a subscription when you open an Office file.

#270. Trump FCC declares California isn't allowed to enforce phone service rules

FCC preempts state rules that require AT&T to keep offering home phone service.

The Federal Communications Commission ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT&T, setting up another battle between the Trump administration and California over the state’s right to enforce its own telecom laws and regulations.

AT&T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort in California requires it to offer telephone service to any potential customer in its territory. AT&T wants to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.

The order released today granted AT&T’s request to preempt state rules, following up on the FCC’s previous approval of AT&T’s petition to discontinue service. AT&T had tried to achieve the same result in court, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.

The FCC order probably isn’t the last word, as California could sue the commission. California has stood alone against AT&T, which has received relief from COLR obligations in 20 of the 21 states in its wireline service territory.

“California’s Carrier of Last Resort framework may have made sense when it was established 30 years ago,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement released with today’s order. “But those rules were designed for a bygone era and no longer make sense in today’s competitive, advanced marketplace.”

If AT&T ends service on its old copper lines, many homes and businesses would not be offered modern fiber networks. AT&T claims a wireless home phone service that connects to the cellular network will be good enough, and the FCC agreed.

“The FCC has granted AT&T’s applications to replace legacy voice service with a modern, IP-based alternative in certain areas of the state. California’s state requirements are blocking AT&T from proceeding with a federally authorized transition,” Carr said.

California says its rules allow wireless replacements if they meet the state’s standards for basic phone service, but that AT&T must demonstrate that its wireless phone service would meet the COLR obligations. California’s requirements include flat-rate options for unlimited voice calls, discounted Lifeline rates for eligible low-income customers, and telephone relay service for people who are deaf and hard of hearing.

FCC Democrat Anna Gomez voted against the order, saying that state telecom commissions “are often the last line of defense for consumers. They know their communities, they take their complaints, and they answer to the people who rely on these services in a way that a federal agency in Washington cannot always match.”

Gomez said the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) has an open proceeding on how to modernize its COLR rules, and that the FCC should let that process play out. Large technology transitions work best “when the state regulator is a partner with a real role,” but the FCC is treating the CPUC “as an obstacle to be cleared,” she said.

The CPUC “proceeding is the right place for California to weigh what a modern basic service requirement should look like, with input from the people who will actually be making that switch,” Gomez said. “AT&T has said it does not plan to discontinue service before June 1, 2027, which leaves time for the CPUC to finish its work. Rather than wait, this item tells the CPUC to write its new consumer protections around a federal ruling it opposed.”

In March, the FCC issued an order that made it easier for carriers to discontinue copper networks. The order asserted that state rules are subject to preemption if they conflict with the FCC’s discontinuance authorizations and authority. AT&T cited the order in its lawsuit against California.

Trump officials and telecom companies have been trying to block California’s rules for years. The first Trump administration lost an attempt to preempt state net neutrality laws throughout the country in 2019, and California later defeated ISPs in a lawsuit that challenged its net neutrality law in court.

California’s net neutrality law and other telecom regulations are again being threatened by rules the Trump administration applied to federal grants, but California rejected US demands to stop enforcing its laws this month. In that case, California may have to choose between enforcing its telecom laws and receiving $1.42 billion to deploy broadband to 270,571 locations.

#268. Should you go with a headphone DAC/amp combo or a stack?

Both will do a fine job, and it depends on what you need from your gear.

You don't always need a DAC and amp to enjoy music through headphones. If your computer or laptop's headphone jack already delivers clean audio at a comfortable volume, then you're probably fine. Some MacBooks from 2021 and later, for example, support both low- and high-impedance headphones and can deliver up to 3 volts RMS through their headphone jacks when you use headphones rated between 150 and 1,000 ohms. If your headphone jack isn't quite as capable, or if you're not satisfied with the sound, though, then it's time to spend on some hardware.

A DAC and a headphone amp can come together in a single unit (usually known as a DAC/amp) or as a stack of separate units. And while the latter seems like the more serious setup, it doesn't necessarily mean you'll enjoy a better listening experience. The main job of a DAC is to turn digital audio signals into analog signals, while the amplifier takes those analog signals and makes them loud enough to power your headphones. Both a DAC/amp combo and a stack do the same thing, and which you go for largely depends on your headphones, how much flexibility you need and, of course, your budget.

For most listeners, a DAC/amp is the way to go, especially if you're trying to improve your computer's audio without taking up too much space. Not only is a single unit more convenient, but it also means fewer cables dangling around and one less power adapter to worry about. You can even use a portable USB-C DAC/amp dongle designed for smartphones, but desktop versions usually offer better connectivity and power.

DAC/amps can also offer better value than separates, too. Schiit's Magni 6 sells for $169 with its optional internal USB DAC. Conversely, you can buy the Magni 6 sans DAC for $99 and pair it with the Modi 5 DAC for $149 (or $164 with a power adapter). That brings the total to over $250, and you don't even get an interconnect cable. The Modi 5 has optical and coaxial inputs, sure, but that doesn't automatically equate to better sound.

DAC/amp combos don't necessarily have to come with major compromises, either. The $549 JDS Labs Element IV delivers up to 3.2 watts per channel into 32 ohms, and comes with features like automatic gain switching, EQ and even preamp outputs for powered speakers. That's more than enough for many demanding headphones, eliminating the need for a dedicated amplifier. The downside, of course, is that you're stuck with the combo and can't upgrade piecemeal.

While DAC/amp combos are great, a stack can still make sense for audiophiles who use a wide variety of headphones or who like to tinker with their hi-fi setup. Going with separates gives you the freedom to upgrade the amplifier down the line without giving up a perfectly capable DAC, or vice versa.

Certain headphones may also benefit from the power a dedicated amp can provide. Some high-impedance headphones just ask for a lot of power, while planar magnetic models, for example, can combine low impedance and low sensitivity. Let's take the HiFiMAN Susvara Unveiled, for example, which has a 45-ohm impedance and only 86 dB sensitivity. The Absolute Sound advises at least 6 watts of amplification, so a standalone amp may be the better choice here. However, too much power can be a bad thing, too: a very powerful amp may result in audible hiss with very sensitive headphones. So start by checking your headphones' power requirements and the amplifier's noise performance instead of just assuming that you need a beefy amp.

You may also get extra analog inputs, more gain settings or extra headphone outputs (such as balanced connectors) when you go for a dedicated amplifier. This extra flexibility is not unique to separates, but you're more likely to get these bonuses with a dedicated amp. There is, however, a price to pay for these perks, as higher-end headphone amps like Topping's $499 A70 Pro can cost more than many DAC/amps on their own. You'll also have to deal with the potential hassle of accommodating a pair of interconnects and an extra power cable. It's unavoidable if you need what a stack offers, but not everyone will.

#267. This free 'Swiss Army Knife' for macOS can replace your utility apps

Vorssaint is a powerful, modular utility suite, provided permissions are carefully managed.

macOS offers one of the most refined desktop experiences, but users looking for more granular control of their desktops might find the OS' native options limiting. Unlike Microsoft's PowerToys, which includes a collection of over 25 productivity and customization tools, Mac users must often turn to a fragmented selection of third-party applications to achieve similar levels of control. For example, macOS' native window tiling is serviceable at best, allowing for only a few tiling options regardless of screen size. Similarly, the OS doesn't natively support independent volume control and output device selection for individual applications. This is where Vorssaint, the Swiss Army Knife of macOS utility apps, comes into the picture.

Vorssaint is a third-party, open source application that aims to resolve macOS' productivity and customization pain points with a single menu-bar application. The app groups together a range of utility tools and nifty quick toggles to streamline productivity. The project is hosted on GitHub, and has earned over 33,000 stars and 230 contributors.

Vorssaint includes an impressive collection of utilities that aims to improve how users interact with their Macs. Its window-tiling feature offers more control over how users arrange their application windows, including edge snapping and shortcuts. The app also includes a toggle for clamshell mode, enabling MacBooks to continue running even with their lids closed, while its "Keep Awake" feature allows users to control when or if their Macs can enter a sleep state.

The application suite also includes several handy tools that streamline daily workflows. For example, its screenshot utility supports scrolling screenshots, which makes it possible to capture content that extends beyond what's visible on the screen. Users can also edit captured screenshots with the app's in-built image editing tool. Similarly, Vorssaint's media tool is capable of video compression, image conversion and text extraction from images. Meanwhile, its system monitoring tool extends beyond Mac's Activity Monitor, providing valuable information on thermals, memory usage and network speed.

These are just a few examples of what Vorssaint offers. The suite also includes a graphical interface for Homebrew, URL cleaner and a powerful command bar. The command bar is akin to Apple's Spotlight search, but a lot more exciting. Its functionality extends beyond just searching apps and files; it can also be used to perform quick mathematical calculations, unit conversions and access most of Vorssaint's utilities by simply searching for them.

Vorssaint's robust utility stack undoubtedly makes it a promising productivity suite for power users. However, some of its powerful tools require sensitive macOS permissions. Depending on what features users install, the app may request permissions for Accessibility, Screen Recording, Full Disk Access and Automation. While granting these permissions is necessary to allow Vorssaint to perform some of its functions like taking screenshots, uninstalling applications and other system-level operations, users must understand what it means to grant system-level permissions to applications, especially those built by third-party developers.

This is where Vorssaint's modular design becomes particularly useful, allowing users to choose specific modules according to their requirements. For example, someone particularly interested in streamlining window management can choose to install only the Window layout module, and need not grant it screen recording and app management permissions. This selective approach lets users retain the modules they without having to risk granting sensitive permissions.

#265. “Race realism” isn’t realistic—and it isn’t good science

Modern genetics does not support claims of innate racial differences in intelligence.

At this year’s World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, US President Donald Trump stated that people from Somalia have low IQs. “I always say these are low-IQ people,” he said in his speech. His son, Donald Trump Jr, made a similar statement about Haitian people in 2024 (Trump’s government has since ended the protected status of both Somali and Haitian migrants in the US).

These statements and their consequences are symptoms of a growing trend in Western politics: the re-emergence of racial views of human nature that have been largely in hiding for the past 70 years. Narratives about the innate intellectual inferiority of black or brown people compared with white people—which can still be found in academic journals today—are fuelling far-right propaganda in some of the world’s largest democracies. Such claims underpin misinformation strategies on social media and bolster political movements.

These narratives are sometimes euphemistically referred to as “race science” or more recently “race realism.” But, as we argue, they are not actually scientific. One member of this community, Nathan Cofnas, recently attracted public attention by accusing the late Jason Arday of plagiarism.

What got less attention was that Cofnas has links to a network of people who make supposedly scientific claims about the innate intelligence, criminality, or sexuality of different racial groups. Some within this network are affiliated with universities, giving their work the mask of legitimacy.

This group produces work that has the appearance of science, but which is methodologically deeply flawed and fails to engage with rigorous scientific research. Yet they regularly succeed in publishing this work in (a handful of) mainstream academic journals.

How do they manage to do this, and what are the consequences?

Contemporary race scientists position themselves as persecuted but legitimate scientists who are prevented from pursuing their work for ideological reasons. They sometimes refer to what they defend as hereditarianism. This is the idea that genetic differences play a key causal role in determining differences in human behavior and intelligence between human groups—such as races—over purely environmental differences.

Yet scientific evidence has shown repeatedly and from many points of view that hereditarian thinking is both flawed and wrong. Race scientists make extremely simplistic claims such as: “Black people have innately lower intelligence than white people, because selection pressures resulted in the evolution of higher intelligence in white people.” No part of this claim can be scientifically supported; not from the point of view of genetics, evolutionary biology, or psychology.

In the 1970s, the influential evolutionary biologist Richard Lewontin famously showed that there is more genetic variation within human groups than between them. Socially defined racial groups just aren’t that genetically different from one another. There is genetic variation—though we’re actually a relatively genetically similar species compared to closely related primates. But this variation doesn’t fall neatly into clusters that correlate with how we typically categorize races.

Skin tone and color do vary between geographical locations. So do some other physiological features like hair texture, or the ability to process oxygen or milk products. But these differences are associated with characteristics of the environment rather than with racial groups. Some genetic variants associated with white skin color, for example, may have originated in Africa. Similarly, the ability to digest milk is seen in some populations in Europe, Africa, and Asia, rather than being an exclusively “Aryan” characteristic, as far right groups sometimes claim.

We now know considerably more about the human genome than Lewontin did in the 1970s, but his conclusions are supported today. Knowing someone’s race just doesn’t tell us a great deal about their genetics.

Recent scientific advances allowing us to examine ancient DNA from archaeological sites help explain why genetic differences do not fall neatly along racial lines. This research paints a picture of constant mixing between human groups, as waves of migration washed to and fro across the globe. It ultimately makes any belief in the genetic “purity” of European or African populations meaningless.

While human genetics is fascinatingly complex, race scientists ignore this complexity in favor of a far-too-simplistic view of humanity. And this view is not supported by the work of scientists who have used rigorous scientific methods to further our understanding of our species.

When race scientists say that black people have lower intelligence than white people, they typically base that on claims of differences in IQ test results. But the data underlying these claims is often shaky, to say the least.

Hereditarians have relied heavily on a database that claims to provide average IQs for countries worldwide: the “national IQ” database. Researchers have repeatedly demonstrated that this database is deeply methodologically flawed. It isn’t possible to measure intelligence in the same way in very different cultures, with different exposure to formal education. That’s because we know that education is one of several other factors linked to differences in IQ.

The methods used to put the database together did not come even close to meeting typical standards of scientific rigor. There’s even analysis suggesting that low IQ samples were deliberately chosen to represent sub-Saharan Africa, to make the IQ for black populations artificially low.

Meanwhile, the Flynn effect, showing that IQ has risen considerably during the 20th and 21st centuries, clearly demonstrates that IQ scores are heavily determined by the environment we’re in. Such a rapid rise over a short period of time must have environmental, not genetic, causes.

What’s more, intelligence is a contested topic—something that is hard to define and measure. IQ tests only measure specific cognitive abilities, ignoring things like social intelligence or creativity, for example. In fact, social intelligence features heavily in mainstream research on the evolution of human intelligence.

As one of us recently outlined in a peer-reviewed paper, race scientists are largely silent on the social brain hypothesis—the view that humans evolved remarkable intellectual abilities to manage social issues. In every group, there is strong social competition around resources, mating, and status. These are the things humans spend the most time navigating—the complexities of our rich social lives.

Not one of the prominent mainstream views on the evolution of human intelligence concludes there are innate cognitive differences between racial groups. Factors that have been put forward range from our cooperative child rearing to our heavy reliance on culture and learning. These all involve our social relationships, and all have received equal lack of attention from race scientists.

Mainstream opinion in the evolutionary behavioral sciences is that cognitively, all human groups are the same, though of course individuals within groups differ. Our amazing behavioral diversity stems from our species’ ability to adapt flexibly to our environment. This is especially because of our reliance on culture and social learning—not because we have evolved different psychologies to suit different environments.

Rather than drawing on this mainstream research, race scientists use simplistic “just-so” stories to explain how race differences in traits such as intelligence supposedly evolved. Their “cold winters theory,” for example, claims that the challenges of cold winters in Europe and east Asia created evolutionary selection pressures for greater intelligence after human groups migrated out of Africa. In doing so, they make unsupportable assumptions about environmental differences between Africa and the rest of the world. They also fail to acknowledge half a century of research on the evolution of human cognitive ability.

Yes, we needed to learn new food gathering practices and methods for dealing with environmental challenges as we migrated across the world. But the same was true as humans migrated across the large and ecologically diverse continent of Africa. Race scientists provide no evidence for their arguments. They don’t rely on archaeological evidence, nor do they use typical methods from evolutionary biology to understand evolutionary processes. Using the methods of race scientists, it would be equally easy to make the argument that challenges posed by hot summers drove the evolution of higher intelligence, and equally without scientific backing.

No matter which way you look at these issues—from the view of genetics, anthropology, evolutionary biology, or psychology—hereditarianism does not hold up.

To understand the potential consequences of these views, it is important to see them in historical context. Early in the 20th century, race science was mainstream. Overly simplistic and biologically deterministic views about the origins of differences between human groups—not just race but class—were widespread (if not universal) and important to the eugenics movement.

If disadvantaged groups owe their disadvantage to some fault within them, and not to the structural conditions they experience, then some argue society is not responsible for helping those people. Such arguments led to eugenic sterilization laws that aimed to “improve” society by preventing—without their consent—the reproduction of those considered likely to pass on their innate “defects” to future children. And it was ultimately behind the Nazis’ “solution” of trying to eliminate “undesirables” entirely.

In the decades after the Second World War, the horrors of the Nazi regime led to a decline in the popularity of eugenics in mainstream research and a rejection of race science. But the belief that science supported eugenic claims was already collapsing, even as the Nazis were trying to implement a race-based society. As we learned more about human biology and genetics during the 20th century, it became obvious that human genetic variation was too complex to be mapped into socially recognized racial (or class) categories. Advances in science meant race science dropped out of mainstream thinking.

Yet those committed to a belief in a biological hierarchy of races, regardless of what the science said, wanted venues in which they could continue their discussions. In the 1960s, the pseudo-scientific journal Mankind Quarterly became their venue. Mankind Quarterly was funded by the Pioneer Fund, a nonprofit foundation set up in the 1930s by a US textile magnate who chose to use his fortune to fund research on race science and fight desegregation in the US.

The Pioneer Fund continued to fund race science into the 21st century—including supporting Mankind Quarterly—when it was taken over by the current network of race scientists. They channeled its remaining funds into a new company, the Human Diversity Foundation, subsequently rebranded as Polygenic Scores LLC.

Given all this, how is race science still being published in mainstream academic journals? To be clear, race science does not typically get published in genetics or evolutionary biology journals. Most academic journals operate peer review, meaning papers only get published after evaluation by experts in the field. The overall absence of race science in genetics or biology journals is a clear signal that it does not meet contemporary standards of scientific rigor in genetics or biology.

Instead, race scientists continue to publish in para-scientific journals. But race science also makes it into a growing number of mainstream social science or humanities journals. Psychologist Andrew Winston, an expert in the history of race science in psychology, has described it as a “community project… with its own networks, mentorships, journals, funding, conferences, heroes, origin myths, martyrs, defenders, and historiography.”

Behind the network of writers producing race science sits a community of editors, peer reviewers, and others in gatekeeping roles, which too often allows race science to be published in mainstream journals. This is particularly in the subfields of psychology interested in intelligence and individual differences, and evolutionary psychology.

Editors of Intelligence, the mainstream journal that has probably published the largest quantity of race science, have occasionally published editorials defending their publication of race science in the name of ensuring robust academic debate even on controversial topics.

There have been sanctions. Philippe Rushton, one of an earlier generation of race scientists, faced sanctions from his university in Canada but kept his job apparently owing to the intervention of Edward O. Wilson, arguably the most famous biologist toward the end of the 20th century.

Cofnas created justified controversy over his call for a “hereditarian revolution” after which it will be acknowledged that black people are innately intellectually disadvantaged compared to white people. But he kept his postdoctoral fellowship at Cambridge University (though his affiliation with a Cambridge college was ended). He has also kept his postdoctoral position at Ghent University after using the opportunity provided by excessive news coverage of Arday to publicize his hereditarian views (though some sanctions have been imposed, such as restrictions on teaching). Cofnas has defended his views by saying he’s been misunderstood and is entitled to free inquiry.

Moreover, when University College London discovered that the race science community had been holding conferences on its premises (the “London Conferences on Intelligence”), without their knowledge of the subject of the conferences, they acted to prevent further such conferences being held. The publisher of the journal Intelligence, Elsevier, has recently appointed new editors, who have stated their commitment to publishing both rigorous and socially responsible science. Race scientists are increasingly publishing in evolutionary psychology journals rather than Intelligence.

However, the London Conferences on Intelligence continue, though not at UCL. Race scientists also have a media arm, Aporia magazine, which promotes race science using much more overt language and with more obvious policy focus than publications in academic journals. One Aporia article, for example, argued for eugenics as a solution to Africa’s lack of economic development, noting in a post that some may find it “distasteful.” It claimed—relying on race science’s unscientific arguments—that artificial selection for higher intelligence is needed to improve the continent’s innately unintelligent populace.

Race science may not have the respect of the scientific community, but it does have funding and influential backers. A report by Hope not Hate revealed that the network of race scientists received significant funding from the US businessman Andrew Conru, who withdrew his funding after the report was released.

The US Ambassador to Belgium even intervened when Ghent University set up an investigation into how Cofnas was hired.

Race scientists are far from the victims they claim to be. Race scientists in this and previous generations have worked hard to ensure their messages are heard beyond academia. And in this generation, they are successfully using social media to spread their beliefs, especially Elon Musk’s X.

But what about academic freedom? Isn’t it good for science to discuss any hypothesis to ensure free exchange of ideas? Academic debate is productive only if it involves methodologically rigorous research. Science will not progress if one side of any debate consistently uses poor-quality, methodologically flawed work. Nor is it necessary to continually debate topics that have long since been settled.

We believe it is unequivocal that race science is fundamentally pseudoscience. In our view, it’s critical to call attention to not only the scientific flaws underlying this body of work but also the real target it’s aimed at: political actors and everyday readers who ultimately decide the direction that science, and society, goes in.

Jonathan R. Goodman is Assistant Research Professor, Psychiatry, University of Cambridge, and Rebecca Sear is Director of the Centre for Culture and Evolution, Brunel University of London.

#264. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

#263. How to clear your cache on Google TV

It's worth trying if you're having issues.

If you're experiencing slow performance or other issues with your Google TV, you may have heard about clearing the cache. Caches generally help Android devices such as Google TVs run more smoothly by storing data — such as TV show thumbnails — that may need to be accessed quickly later. While this may not be an issue on a device with plenty of storage, very few Google TV devices have more than the bare minimum there. The Google TV Streamer that replaced the Chromecast has 32GB of space, the bare minimum for an Android device, making cache management all the more important.

Even though Google TV manages app caches automatically, they can still get too large, especially if you have a lot of apps installed or store large video files on the TV or streaming box. App caches can also bloat or get corrupted, causing issues including slow performance, app crashes and frustrating system glitches.

Thankfully, Android makes it easy to clear the cache, whether for individual apps or all installed apps, through its settings menu. If your Google TV has become sluggish or glitchy over time, clearing the cache is a troubleshooting step you shouldn't skip.

There are two ways to clear your Google TV cache: system-wide or per-app. If you're experiencing slowdowns or other issues across the entire operating system, use the former option. The latter is best for when only a single app is giving you trouble.

To clear the cache system-wide, open Google TV settings by going to the home screen, holding down the home button on your remote or selecting your profile icon, and selecting the gear icon at the top of the quick settings panel. Go to System > Storage > Internal shared storage > Cached data, then select OK to clear the cached data for all of the apps on your device.

If only one app is acting up, clearing all the cache is overkill. Instead, go to Settings using the steps in the above paragraph, then select Apps > See all apps. Scroll to find and select the app you're having issues with, then select Force Stop and confirm by selecting OK. Next, select Clear Cache and confirm by selecting OK. If you still have issues, it's worth clearing the cache system-wide using the above steps. If even that doesn't work, try rebooting the Google TV. Finally, if you still have trouble, go back to the app's settings page and clear both its cache and data. This will erase everything and return the app to its default state, so only use it as a last resort.

While clearing the cache for all apps system-wide can make your Google TV device more responsive in the short term, it's a temporary fix for the real problem: insufficient storage. As noted earlier, Google TV devices rarely come with that much storage, and installing dozens of apps will quickly eat through it.

It's generally good practice to keep approximately 10 percent of an Android device's storage empty. This buffer gives the system breathing room for operations that keep the drive healthy and to build robust app caches. If your Google TV storage is too full, clearing the cache likely won't resolve all your performance issues.

After clearing the system-wide cache, go to Settings > System > Storage > Internal Shared Storage to see how much space your apps, movies, photos and other files are taking up. The remaining free space will be shown at the bottom. If 90 percent or more of the drive is full, it's time to start deleting things.

If media is the culprit, back the files up and delete them. For most Google TVs, though, the space-hogging culprit is likely installed apps. A good way to start is by deleting any apps you haven't used in a long time, especially if they're taking up an inordinate amount of space. Keeping that streaming service you downloaded to watch a single movie isn't worth the frustration of dealing with a slow TV.

#261. Here's how much Starlink cost in 2020 vs. 2026

Starlink's cheapest home plan costs $44 less per month than it did in 2020, but hardware ownership and regional pricing have changed.

Starlink rolled out its public beta in October 2020, with the equipment costing $499 and the monthly subscription $99. Six years down the road, SpaceX's satellite internet service starts at $55 monthly for US customers, with equipment rentals available at no upfront cost in select areas. That's $44 less a month, or $528 less annually, on the subscription cost alone.

The company also jacked up its residential rates in 2026, but the entry-level rate is still lower than it was in 2020. Throw in discounts and fluctuating rates based on local demand, and two customers could end up paying vastly different bills for the same satellite internet service.

SpaceX's first public beta was rolled out as the "Better Than Nothing Beta." True to its very transparent (and accurate) name, customers were asked to expect download speeds of 50 to 150 Mbps and latency of 20 to 40ms, paired with occasional periods of zero connectivity.

The hardware kit with the price tag of $499 included Starlink's original circular satellite dish, a mounting tripod and a Wi-Fi router. With the first $99 monthly subscription payment, the initial cost came to $598, excluding shipping and taxes. So if the monthly rate remained the same, the first year's total would've been $1,687, including the equipment.

What customers with reliable broadband might scoff at, though, could still be an acceptable price for those stuck with slow DSL or unreliable cellular service, even with occasional outages.

SpaceX did hike the monthly rates to $110 back in March 2022, and it took effect for current users in April 2022. The hardware cost also went up to $599 for new users and $549 for customers with existing deposits. The culprit, according to the company, was inflation. In 2023, there were two prices for residential subscriptions: $90 in areas where there was excess network capacity and $120 in areas where there was limited network capacity.

The satellite internet service is now available with three primary residential plans: Residential 100 Mbps for $55 per month, Residential 200 Mbps for $85 and Residential Max at $130. Each plan offers unlimited data, but the first two are locked to speed limits. The Max plan does get higher network priority and claims speeds of 400 Mbps or higher in suitable conditions.

Starlink can be more expensive than cable, fiber or 5G home internet, but availability is where the value lies. The company's portable Roam service is available at $55 for 100GB of high-speed internet, after which speeds go down. If you don't want the high-speed data cap, Roam Unlimited costs $175 per month.

#260. New EU budget proposal aims at tax gobal tech giants

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a smaller EU budget for 2028-2034, including a 3% tax on major digital firms to ease member states' contributions. France has already rejected the plan as inadequate.

European Council President Antonio Costa has proposed a new draft for the next EU budget.

Among other things, he is suggesting a tax on big tech firms to ease the contributions of member states, some of which strongly criticised earlier proposals.

The EU budget is theEuropean Union’s shared budget and it is used for things ranging from agricultural subsidies, infrastructure projects to border control and defence.

A first draft for the 2028 to 2034 budget was proposed by the EU Commission in 2025 but was criticised, especially by a group of northern European members including Germany who wanted the budget to be much smaller.

Following that criticism, the European Council President has now suggested a new draft, which is smaller by €204 billion.

But divisions among member states appear to remain, with France immediately coming out against Costa’s new draft, saying it was "deeply disappointing."

The proposal includes a string of new "revenue channels," explicitly intended to "to keep national contributions at a reasonable level," so that member state will have to contribute less than otherwise would be the case.

The biggest splash would likely come from a tax on companies with an annual turnover from digital activities of at least 50 million euros in the EU and 750 million euros worldwide.

Those firms would be subject to "an annual contribution corresponding to 3% of the annual net turnover from online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data," according to Costa.

Aside from the tech tax, the "balanced basket of new own resources" also includes taxes on tobacco products and electronic waste.

Neither the EU Commission nor European Council President Costa will have the final word on the budget. Costa's plan will now be at the centre of hours of talks when EU leaders meet in Brussels next week.

"This is a realistic budget that addresses our new priorities while preserving our established policies," Costa wrote about his proposal. "I am confident that this proposal is a good basis for moving towards a final agreement."

But an initial reaction from France suggests that any final agreement might still be some way off.

The French presidency said the budget "falls well short ​of ‌what is needed, particularly on ‌the Common Agricultural Policy, ‌notably ​to guarantee income support for farmers."

"As it ⁠stands, ​this proposal ​from the President ​of the European ‌Council does not ​provide ⁠a basis for an ⁠agreement."

The EU was hoping to reach a general agreement on the budget by the end of 2026 with its formal adoption planned for 2027.

#259. Review: Godzilla Minus Zero joins the list of truly stellar sequels

Director Takashi Yamazaki ups the ante by pitting Godzilla against one of the monster’s greatest foes

It’s a rare thing for a film sequel to match or even surpass its predecessor; The Godfather Part II and Terminator 2: Judgement Day are the best known examples on a pretty short list. Go ahead and add Godzilla Minus Zero to that list. Director Takashi Yamazaki’s sequel to his critically acclaimed Godzilla Minus One (2023) is everything one could want in a Godzilla movie: human pathos, great special effects, and, ultimately, two giant kaiju duking it out over who gets to destroy Japan (and eventually the world) the most.

(Spoilers for the first film below. Spoilers for Minus Zero but no major reveals until after the gallery. We’ll give you a heads-up when we get there.)

As I wrote previously, Yamazaki wanted to return to Godzilla’s filmic roots with Minus One, setting the events in postwar Japan and tapping into the monster’s symbolic representation of the Japanese perspective on the 1940s nuclear holocaust—while also incorporating all-too-human themes of guilt and redemption. That first film focused on kamikaze pilot Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who struggled with survivor’s guilt after he failed to take action when Godzilla attacked the Japanese base on Odo Island in 1945.

Knocked unconscious, Kōichi survived and awoke to find his parents and many others were killed in the World War II bombing of Tokyo. Kōichi rebuilt a life with a woman named Noriko (Minami Hamabe) and the orphaned baby she rescued, Akiko (Sae Nagatani). But then Godzilla re-emerged, and Kōichi resolved to die fighting the monster to atone for Odo Island. Kōichi saved the day and lived to tell the tale. He reunited with Noriko, who had a strange black bruise on her neck. And we saw a chunk of Godzilla’s remains start to regenerate, leaving things open for a sequel.

Godzilla Minus One was a massive hit, both in Japan—where it remains one of the highest grossing Japanese films ever—and worldwide, racking up $116 million globally and winning an Oscar for best visual effects. Yamazaki said in interviews at the time that there had as yet been no talk of a sequel—while also hinting at future directions a sequel might explore. He later admitted it was way of planting a seed for what would become Godzilla Minus Zero.

Godzilla Minus Zero is set two years after the events of the first film, with Kamiki and Hamabe reprising their roles as Kōichi and Noriko, along with Nagatani as Akiko. The family is just trying to live in peace after the devastation Godzilla inflicted on their country. Alas, a new kaiju emerges, arriving via meteorite and using its tentacles to feed on local wildlife before morphing into a dragon-like creature that causes fresh rampaging destruction. Fans of the genre will recognize this creature as Ghidorah, whose appearance in the film was teased in the various trailers.

It isn’t long before Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka)—i.e., the dude with the magnificent wavy gray hair who is director of the Large-Scale Disaster Response Bureau—seeks out Kōichi for help in dealing with this new kaiju threat. His team is able to track Ghidorah’s movements via electrical storms and other pertinent weather patterns, thanks to meteorologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa). But the team has no idea how they might defeat this new threat to life and infrastructure. It’s hardly a spoiler to note that at some point, a regenerated Godzilla will come into play.

(WARNING: significant spoilers appear below. Stop reading now if you haven’t seen the film.)

Yamazaki has retained the visual tone that made the film’s predecessor so striking; it feels like classic Godzilla fare of yore, just with 21st century cutting-edge visual effects. If anything, he’s upped his game on the special effects front, reflecting the larger production budget he had to work with. (It’s also the first Japanese movie filmed specifically for IMAX and it’s well-worth seeing in that format.)

Much of that budget went toward bringing the central monsters to cinematic life, and Godzilla Minus Zero does not disappoint. Ghidorah, for instance, responds to a bombing attack by mutating into its famous three-headed King Ghidorah form, complete with a spiffy new superpower: a “gravity beam” that lets the creature levitate entire houses (and, at one point, Godzilla) into the sky before dropping them back to the ground. And the kaiju vs. kaiju battle is spectacular in both scope and execution.

Yamazaki even managed to squeeze in what he called his “bucket-list” special effects shot inspired by a scene in 2008’s Cloverfield: Godzilla looming out of the Atlantic Ocean in front of the Statue of Liberty to wreck havoc on the statue and New York City in general. Granted, it occurs in a dream sequence of biologist Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka), who survived the Hiroshima blast that killed his wife and children and longs for revenge. And it’s not just indulgence on the director’s part: the scene reinforces the traditional theme of linking Godzilla to nuclear radiation and the horrors of the atomic bomb.

Nor does Yamazaki ignore the human factor via the dilemma of his nuclear family trio. Kōichi must wrestle with his conscience: how can he risk his life again to battle a kaiju when it could mean leaving Akiko an orphan yet again should he fail? Noriko is infected with Godzilla’s radioactive G-cells—the only human to survive the mutations in her own body for so long. But her time could be running out, plus they’ve kept her infection secret for fear she will be taken away by the government for experimentation. Sometimes doing the right thing comes at great personal cost, and watching these quite ordinary people grapple with that reality brings emotional depth to the film.

The film ends on a suitably bittersweet note, and while Yamazaki hasn’t dropped any hints about a possible third film in the series, we’d love to learn more about Noriko’s strangely symbiotic connection to Godzilla via the G-cells in her bloodstream. Long may he reign.

Godzilla Minus Zero is still playing in theaters.

#257. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.
