#220. Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?

For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.

The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.

Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”

Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.

Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.

The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.

This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.

In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”

Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”

But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?

Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female. Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.

Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “LICENSE YOUR FACE” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.

A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”

Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”

How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.

A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”

For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.

Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.

“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”

Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.

Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators team up with a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.

Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”

Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

#219. Dozens missing as deadly fire hits Indonesian candy factory

At least three people were killed in a devastating fire at a confectionery factory on Java. Officials said many more people remain unaccounted for, prompting fears of a much larger tragedy.

Indonesian rescue teams are searching for 37 workers who remained unaccounted for after a fire at a candy-making factory killed at least three people, officials said on Sunday.

The fire occurred at the Fonusa Agung Mulia factory on Java, around 50 kilometers (31 miles) west of the capital, Jakarta.

Footage from the scene showed workers' family members waiting for news.

The factory caught fire on Saturday afternoon, local search and rescue agency official Rizky Dwianto said.

"All elements of the joint SAR (search-and-rescue) team are making maximum effort to locate the victims while prioritizing the safety of personnel in the field," he added.

Rizky said four people injured in the blaze had been taken to a nearby hospital and health clinic. Eleven more were said to have been rescued alive, with dozens of others still missing.

The authorities deployed 15 fire trucks to the scene, along with a rescue team including the police, the military, the Red Cross and volunteers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Authorities said the blaze had largely been contained as of Sunday. However, firefighters were still carrying out intensive cooling operations to allow access all parts of the factory, according to Tubagus Mahfud, the operations chief of the district fire department.

He noted there were still hot spots in some parts of the building.

"We are conducting sweeps in the areas that have already been brought under control," Mahfud said. "Parts of the structure had collapsed, while poor lighting conditions required firefighters to proceed cautiously."

Drone footage shows the fire destroyed large sections of the three-story building, bringing down the roof in some places.

Survivors said the fire started in a cooling unit on the third floor.

The exact death toll was not immediately clear. While three people were confirmed to be dead, a report by the Reuters news agency indicated police removed 24 body bags from the scene.

Separately, the company's CEO said around 300 people were on site on Saturday, with 65 workers believed to be in the affected area when the fire broke out.

Senior police official in charge of victims' identification, Wahyu Hidayati Dwi Palupi, urged family members to provide DNA samples and other information to identify the victims, warning that the victims' condition made visual identification impossible.

The factory, located in the Serang district of Banten province, produces Milkita, an Indonesian brand of milk-based candies and snack products exported to over 40 countries worldwide.

The blaze marks only the latest in Indonesia's series of deadly industrial fires in recent years, raising questions about the country's workplace safety standards.

Among other disasters, at least 22 people were killed in a fire last December that broke out in a seven-story building in Jakarta after a suspected drone battery explosion, police said.

An explosion in a nickel-processing plant in the east of the country killed at least 13 people in 2023.

Microsoft and the US government agree there are more outages to come.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Over the last week or so, we have seen a nationwide FAA ground stop, a multi-day Outlook outage that brought entire companies to a standstill, and a banking outage at JPMorgan Chase. But the consensus is that there are more to come. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN:

“The American people should be prepared for a great deal of investment in upgrading our systems; they should be prepared for investment in cybersecurity, and they should be prepared that any time there is a step change in technology, a step change in both compute and applications, there will be bumps in the road.”

Microsoft President Brad Smith issued a similar warning about further outages on CBS News’ Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan, but sounded a much more ominous tone.

“I think we have to be prepared, frankly, for the coming months because this isn’t the type of thing that just gets done in a couple of weeks … The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now.”

While the outages over the last week were not believed to be caused by cyberattacks, Smith said that AI has made it easier to find flaws, “and then you can either use that knowledge to patch the code, or if you’re a bad actor, you can use that knowledge to try to hack into systems,” he said.

The last few months have also seen an increase in attacks on government and commercial systems, including those at the USDA, JP Morgan, and supermarkets.

Whether outages are brought on by AI-assisted hackers or human error during the rush to patch an aging system, one thing seems certain: there will be more in the coming months.

#214. Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages

Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.

While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.

Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Ask Proxy’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.

It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.

Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.

There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”

The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.

Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.

Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.

Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.

It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.

Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.

The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.

One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.

Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.

Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.

According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”

Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.

Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.

Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.

The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.

Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.

Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.

It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.

Maverick describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.

It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.

The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use.

It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month,  20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.

Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.

Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.

It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.

Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.

Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.

Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details.

There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.

Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.

Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.

Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information.

The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date.

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.

Szn is designed to coordinate tasks and follow-ups through a single conversation thread. Users can send text messages, voice notes, photos, or forwarded emails, and the assistant takes action on their behalf, including making calls, sending emails, and managing follow-ups.

According to the company’s website, Szn has served more than 7,500 businesses across 16 countries, completed over 10,000 jobs, and handled 95 hours of calls.

Tab allows users to delegate everyday tasks through familiar messaging platforms. Users can send requests to the assistant via iMessage or WhatsApp, ranging from ordering groceries to finding birthday gifts, and Tab handles the process on their behalf.

The company emerged from stealth in early October with a valuation of $300 million. Its investors include SV Angel, Valar Ventures, and American Spirit.

The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations.

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.

The basic plan starts at $19.99 per month.

Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives users a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms.

In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.

The company plans to offer the app for free initially and has stated that it will never include advertising.

Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials.

Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.

Fo launched publicly in September 2026 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

#213. India: Nepal PM Balendra Shah heads to Delhi for first bilateral visit

Nepal's rapper-turned-prime minister Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for his first foreign bilateral trip since taking office. He is expected to discuss flood recovery, trade and energy in his talks with Modi. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of the main headlines from India on Saturday, November 21 and Sunday, November 22:

But follow us for more, as we will be back with the latest from across India.

India declared at 720-9, the highest Test total by any team in New Zealand, on day four of the first Test in Wellington.

The innings gave India a 352-run first-innings lead. India's previous best in New Zealand was 520 all out in Hamilton in 2009.

Rishabh Pant struck 128 from 153 balls, his ninth Test century and fourth since returning to Test cricket in 2024. Dhruv Jurel added 78, and the declaration came midway through the second session.

Pant's sixes took him to 108 in Tests, behind only England's Ben Stokes: "I just keep it simple most of the time. Whenever I see the ball, I try to hit it," he said.

New Zealand closed on 119-2, still 233 behind, with Devon Conway unbeaten on 59 and Rachin Ravindra on 27. Jasprit Bumrah dismissed captain Tom Latham for a duck early in the innings, and Henry Nicholls, who made 175 not out in the first innings, fell for 31 to a sharp catch by Jurel off Prasidh Krishna.

New Zealand now need to bat out most of the final day, and India have at least 90 overs to take eight wickets.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah is set to arrive in New Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, his first bilateral trip since taking office in March.

The 36-year-old former rapper will meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday. He will also meet Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and briefly visit President Droupadi Murmu.

Reconstruction after August's devastating floods is expected to dominate the talks. The disaster left some 1,500 dead and more than 5,200 missing, with roads, bridges, power plants, farms and homes destroyed.

Nepal estimates rebuilding will cost $4.78 billion.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nepal is also pressing for an extra route for commercial flights to Bhairahawa and Pokhara.

"India is a major and important partner for Nepal," Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai told reporters, saying the leaders would discuss trade, transit, investment, energy, connectivity and infrastructure.

New Delhi said the visit "reflects the importance India attaches to its relations with Nepal," AFP reported. Local media reported that talks may also touch upon unresolved border disputes.

India is Nepal's largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60% of its imports, worth $8.6 billion, versus China's 13%, according to World Bank figures. India and China regularly compete for influence in Nepal.

Shah will be accompanied by Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle and Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal.

Hello! We are back with the latest news from India this Sunday.

Nepal's rapper-turned-prime minister Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for his first bilateral foreign visit since taking office.

Meanwhile, India has posted a record total of 720-9 on the fourth day of the first cricket test against New Zealand.

We're logging off today, but we will be back tomorrow with the latest from across India.

Workers of the Indian Youth Congress (IYC), the youth wing of the opposition Indian National Congress, protested at US tech giant Meta's offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram on Friday, demanding that the group's leaders' Instagram accounts be restored.

In Hyderabad, protesters entered the building, smashed plants and clashed with police, according to footage the IYC released. Meta declined to comment.

The IYC said Instagram withheld the accounts of its president and in-charge on November 19 "on BJP orders," referring to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, and restored both shortly after the protests.

Manu Jain, who runs the group's social media, told Reuters thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted.

BJP spokesperson Pradeep Bhandari said: "Congress is a party of goons! Goons of Indian Youth Congress are not only vandalized and destroyed Meta's office in Hyderabad, & also are flaunting it on social media!"

Meanwhile, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav warned foreign companies against getting involved in Indian politics.

The Indian government says it orders takedowns only for content that breaches local laws or threatens public safety or national security. In February, it cut the deadline for removing unlawful content from 36 hours to three.

Meta restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India in the first half of 2026, up from about 70,000 in the previous six months, saying most were cases where local law required it to restrict content proactively.

Earlier this month, Brazil’s top electoral court fined Meta's Facebook $1.3 million for failing to comply with judicial orders during the country's presidential election runoff campaign. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's team accused the company of political bias.

India closed day three of the first Test against New Zealand on 486-4, a lead of 118 runs. KL Rahul made 136, Shubman Gill 98 and Rishabh Pant was unbeaten on 55 as every one of India's top five passed 50.

Rahul reached his 13th Test hundred off 207 balls, batting for more than eight hours and sharing stands of 165 with Devdutt Padikkal (80) and 91 with Gill. It completed a set of Test centuries in every major Test-playing nation outside the subcontinent for the Indian wicketkeeper-batsman.

"It feels really awesome, actually, to be able to achieve something like that," Rahul said.

He survived an LBW appeal on 5 that was given not out and New Zealand chose not to review. "Those 15 seconds were probably the slowest 15 seconds of my life," he said of the review process.

Gill and Pant added 100 in the final session before Gill was bowled by Jacob Duffy just before stumps. Duffy finished with 1-180 from 29 overs, the fourth most expensive figures in New Zealand's Test history, AFP said.

The pitch, green on day one, flattened out. "We expected a lot of grass on the wicket, we expected a lot of movement and it has probably not panned out that way," Padikkal said.

New Zealand were all out for 368 in their first innings.

The two-match series ends next week in Christchurch.

At least 14 people have died and more than 200 have been hospitalized after drinking suspected adulterated liquor in Manipur's Chandel district.

At least 12 people remain in critical condition, local media reported.

The victims drank the liquor in the Chakpikarong area, about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from the state capital city of Imphal, and deaths were reported between November 18 and 20.

Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited the hospitals where most patients were being treated on Friday. He ordered an inquiry and said the culprits would be arrested soon.

Police said the liquor came from Sugnu in neighboring Kakching district, with no known local brewing in Chandel. A case has been filed, and two people have been arrested.

The local administration has advised residents not to drink liquor from questionable sources and asked anyone who consumed liquor from the same source to get a medical check-up, even without symptoms.

A US federal judge sentenced an Indian national on Friday to 19 years and seven months in prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

"I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun," he said in court. Judge Victor Marrero said he faces deportation to India after serving his sentence.

Prosecutors say an Indian government employee recruited Gupta in 2023. The government employee remains overseas and is not in US custody.

Gupta paid $15,000 (€13,670) to a person he believed was a hitman, who was actually an undercover US agent.

Prosecutors also said Gupta had told that agent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar's June 2023 killing in Canada that Nijjar "was also the target," the Associated Press reported.

His lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, denied he had any role in the Nijjar killing.

"There is no question he was not the brains behind this operation," she said. Canada has separately alleged India arranged Nijjar's killing, and India dismissed that, with both countries expelling diplomats.

India denies any involvement in the Pannun plot. New Delhi has designated Pannun a terrorist.

Pannun, who leads the group Sikhs for Justice, called Gupta a foot soldier and said outside court: "I'm ready to face India's bullet if that is the price I have to pay."

Hello and welcome to our weekend coverage!

This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest news from and about India.

An Indian national has been sentenced to 19 years and seven months in prison by a US federal judge for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.

Several people have died and more than 200 hospitalized in the northeastern state of Manipur after consuming toxic liquor.

And India has taken a 118-run lead over New Zealand, reaching 486-4 at stumps on day 3 of the first Test against the Black Caps.

#211. Micron Technology: China probes US chip maker for cybersecurity risks as tech tension escalates

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, said it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled new restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it said, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”

Shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based company had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it said last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

#209. Trump says reported FBI database hack is ‘not good’

The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), according to reports in CNN and the Associated Press.

The NCIC is the online database used by federal and local law enforcement to share information about warrants, background checks, and more. The scope of the breach does not yet appear to be clear.

A former FBI official told CNN that they’re not just concerned about “whether hackers gained access to sensitive information, although that is an issue, but whether they could compromise the accuracy of the information that officers rely on.”

President Donald Trump addressed the reports during an interview Saturday with Fox News, saying, “We just heard about it and I will say that it’s not good.” At the same time, Trump also said that as a result of the breach, “maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise because, you know, you had the Russia, Russia, Russia hoax.”

In September, the FBI reportedly told agents and support staff that their personal information had been stolen in a cyberattack.

After expanding its Charmera collection with a Millennium Edition featuring Y2K-inspired designs earlier this year, Reto’s follow-up to its tiny Kodak camera is an equally small digital photo frame you can use to display your shots. But while the Charmera’s usefulness stopped at snapping grainy photos and terrible videos, the Kodak SlideTag goes one step further. It also functions as a Bluetooth tracker that’s compatible with either Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub tracking networks.

The Kodak SlideTag will be available for $34.99 each and, like the Charmera, will feature a series of retro designs distributed in mystery boxes so you don’t know which one you’re going to get. Kodak also sells a complete set of all eight vintage designs for $279.92 if you don’t like mysteries; however, there’s a ninth “secret edition” only available in the individual boxes with a sleek metallic finish.

For those who grew up in an era where projectors are small enough to integrate into phones, the SlideTag is designed to look like a modernized version of the film slides that were used to project photos decades ago. Instead of film, the SlideTag features a 1.54-inch color E Ink screen that mixes six colored inks to display photos at a resolution of 240 x 240.

The color reproduction won’t be as accurate as an LCD or OLED screen, but the SlideTag can hold and cycle up to 12 photos transferred to the device over Bluetooth from Kodak’s Memory Link app running on a mobile device. You can also use it to display a short to-do list, contact details, a countdown timer, or a QR code linking to wherever you want.

As a tracker it’s not quite as functional as an Apple AirTag or Google’s Pixel Tag, which use features like ultra wideband (UWB) and Channel Sounding to make them easier to find. The SlideTag sticks to basic Bluetooth with a range of up to 30 meters out in the open and a 75-decibel buzzer to help locate it when you’re close. Battery life will vary depending on how frequently you use tracking features or refresh the displayed image, but the SlideTag uses a common CR2032 coin cell battery that’s easy to replace.

#207. A tale of two Nvidias

We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.

Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.

And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.

Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.

It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.

Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.

It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”

So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.

Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.

Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.

Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.

Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

#206. US: ICE arrests 2 at Seattle airport in 'chilling' scenes — governor

Washington's governor has denounced the arrests made by ICE officers at Seattle's airport, calling the incident "horrific."

Masked US immigration officers have detained two people on an airport jet bridge in Seattle as passengers boarded a flight to Los Angeles, prompting criticism from Washington state Governor Bob Ferguson and concerns from Alaska Airlines.

The arrests took place at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport around 8 a.m. local time (1600 UTC) on Saturday. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) said the operation targeted Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, a Mexican national who had overstayed his visa.

Agents also arrested Sofia Hernandez Mejia, who they alleged threw hot coffee at the ICE officers during the confrontation. ICE said she had also overstayed her visa and would face a charge of assaulting a federal officer.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Videos of the incident circulated on social media, showing officers struggling with a person on the ground as passengers look on. One woman could be heard shouting that her daughter was being taken away and that she had a work permit.

Governor Ferguson, a Democrat, described the footage as "horrific" and "chilling", accusing ICE of being "completely and totally out of control."

He urged Alaska Airlines to ask federal immigration authorities to leave the state's airports and said he would make the same appeal to other airlines operating at Seattle-Tacoma.

Alaska Airlines said it had received no advance notice of the enforcement operation and was working to understand the circumstances.

The airline also expressed concern over the incident, which it said had been distressing for passengers and employees.

The operation drew criticism from April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, who said it had caused fear and disruption during one of the busiest travel periods of the year.

The flight was delayed, with Alaska Airlines saying many passengers were transferred to other flights. The original service eventually departed at 11 a.m. local time.

#204. Dogecoin jumps after Elon Musk replaces Twitter bird with Shiba Inu

Twitter’s traditional bird icon was booted and replaced with an image of a Shiba Inu, an apparent nod to dogecoin, the joke cryptocurrency that CEO Elon Musk is being sued over.

Musk addressed the change Monday afternoon, tweeting, “as promised” above an image of a year-old conversation in which another user suggested that Musk “just buy Twitter” and “change the bird logo to a doge.”

Elon Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out one account

The doge logo appeared on the site two days after Musk asked a judge to throw out a $258 billion racketeering lawsuit accusing him of running a pyramid scheme to support the dogecoin, according to Reuters.

Lawyers for Musk and Tesla called the lawsuit by dogecoin investors a “fanciful work of fiction” over Musk’s “innocuous and often silly tweets.”

It wasn’t clear whether the logo change was permanent. Musk has been known to use Twitter to troll both his fans and his critics.

The price of dogecoin, which is typically volatile, was up more than 20% over the past 24 hours, to about 9 cents. It was trading just under 8 cents Monday morning.

Dogecoin was created December 6, 2013, by a pair of software engineers — as a joke. The name is a nod to the “doge” meme that became popular a decade ago. Its Shiba Inu mascot mimicks that meme: a dog surrounded by a bunch of Comic Sans text in broken English.

#201. Jensen Huang’s reported affair was ‘most expensive sex since Helen of Troy’, US senator says

John Kennedy looks to Trump leaders as he asks how China evidently bypassed export controls for Nvidia’s top AI chips

Invoking Greek mythology, US senator John Kennedy has characterized former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang’s reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy as “the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy”.

The Louisiana Republican’s allusion to the legendary figure whose desirability was such that it caused the mythic Trojan war came during an interview on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday. Host Kristen Welker asked Kennedy, known for his colloquialisms, if US national security was put at risk by Huang’s affair, given the position his company’s chips have occupied at the forefront of the artificial intelligence boom.

Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s CEO on 12 November after allegations surfaced of extramarital relationships with the suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang and two Nvidia employees.

Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, had been executive director of Megaspeed International. Megaspeed facilitated about $12bn in chip sales, in violation of export controls in the US, where the Trump administration has prohibited the selling of advanced AI chips to China.

On Sunday’s edition of CNN’s State of the Union, the Trump administration’s national intelligence director, Jay Clayton, said he suspected China was able to obtain Nvidia’s most advanced AI chips.

He also said on Fox News Sunday: “There are chips that have ended up in places that they should not.”

Kennedy said he was “less interested in … what [Huang] did” than in asking the Trump administration’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, and its treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, about how China was evidently able to circumvent US “export controls”.

“Mr Huang … did what he did. I hope he had a good time. It was the most expensive sex since Helen of Troy,” Kennedy said.

Lutnick has faced scrutiny over allegedly ignoring warnings that Megaspeed was smuggling chips to China. Other administration leaders, including Bessent, wanted to put Megaspeed on a trade blacklist – but the commerce department stalled enforcement of it.

Kennedy said he could only conclude commerce department leaders are either “so incompetent you wouldn’t put them in charge of a food truck” – or “they knowingly allowed this to happen”.

He said he wanted to get Bessent and Lutnick under oath in front of a Senate committee to “answer some hard questions”.

“And if secretary Lutnick is giving our chips away, he needs to stop it, in my opinion,” Kennedy said.

Bessent said on Sunday’s edition of CBS News’s Face the Nation that the Trump administration had been in touch with Nvidia’s temporary management, lead directors and lawyers while trying to find out who was in charge of compliance at the company.

“It behooves Nvidia to move ⁠quickly on this because we want to know what the culture was,” Bessent said on the program.

Kennedy, a former Louisiana state treasurer who began his political career as a Democrat before switching parties and becoming a staunch Trump administration ally, delivers many of the colloquialisms that have become his calling card with a southern US drawl.

Many believe Kennedy resorts to the drawl to come off as folksy – while he holds degrees from Vanderbilt University, the University of Virginia School of Law and the UK’s Oxford University, and is estimated to be one of the wealthiest US senators.

#200. Abdul El-Sayed doubles down on ‘TrumpCare’ health plan, urging president to ‘get it done’

Democratic senator-elect reiterates suggestion to rename Medicare for All after Trump if president allows bill to pass

Michigan US senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday doubled down on naming healthcare reform legislation after Donald Trump as long as it meant the president would not impede its passage.

“If he’s open to the conversation, I am open to it, too,” El-Sayed said of Trump on Sunday. “If the president is opening to signing that bill, let’s get it done.”

El-Sayed made those remarks on Sunday on NBC’s Meet the Press, where he reiterated his pledge to pursue a single-payer, national healthcare program after the Democrat became the first Muslim person elected to the US Senate during the midterms earlier in November.

Trump’s Republican party is going to lose control of Congress for the second half of his second presidency. But the president has made clear his intention to wield his legislative veto powers whenever he sees fit.

Appearing on Sunday’s Meet the Press, El-Sayed said he would not mind Medicare for All – a big part of his campaign platform – being named “TrumpCare” as long as such a program came into existence.

“I care that the people of this country finally have the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country. And if the president is serious about leaving a lasting legacy, there is nothing better than the ultimate Trump card,” El-Sayed said to Meet the Press host Kristen Welker, making a double entendre for a term that – when the T is lowercase – also refers to a card that beats out others in card games.

El-Sayed told Welker that such a Trump card would be in effect “from the moment [people] are born to the moment that they pass away – that guarantees them the healthcare that has been so elusive in this country without premiums, co-pays and deductibles”.

The senator-elect’s comments come after he previously suggested to CNN that he is not above stroking Trump’s prodigious ego to get legislation passed – including by naming Medicare for All “TrumpCare”.

He also previously wrote on social media, alongside images of a gold health insurance card with “TrumpCare” inscribed on it: “Donald, this is on the table. Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

Trump seemingly responded to El-Sayed’s post by reposting a screenshot of the senator-elect’s tweet. Trump has not formally responded to the push to create universal healthcare.

Trump has spent much of his second presidency trying to get as much as possible named after him – from institutions, physical buildings and currency.

El-Sayed also said that he supports healthcare reform proposed by Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator.

Sanders’ proposal would create a single-payer system in which the federal government insures everybody, financed by an increase in taxes, while eliminating private insurance.

But El-Sayed said he is not focused on eliminating private insurance as an option, which Sanders aims to eliminate by having everything primary and preventive services to hospital stays covered under his proposed plan. Out-of-pocket costs on deductibles and co-pays – staples of the rapacious private insurance industry to which most Americans must resort – would also be eliminated under Sanders’ plan.

El-Sayed said he wants to “provide you basic public health insurance no matter who you are in this country” while being open to the idea of not taking alternative options away.

The senator-elect said he has a meeting on the books with JD Vance. El-Sayed would not share the agenda of the meeting, but he confirmed that the vice-president’s chief of staff contacted him after his election victory.

#199. Can a TV be too large? An investigation

For the past couple of years, I’ve wanted to upgrade my home entertainment situation from the humble trappings of my long sufficient 55-inch TCL smart TV to the model much coveted by cinephiles the world over: the OLED.

The organic light-emitting diode is a specific monitor technology that has really changed the TV industry. Unlike an LED TV, which creates images by shining a backlight through a panel of pixels, OLEDs leverage millions of self-lighting pixels, which provides significantly better pixel control, and can generate a much more nuanced image with deeply vibrant colors and a more intense light and shadows.

They are also significantly more expensive, which is one reason that I’ve held off on investing in one for years. However, this year I couldn’t wait any longer. I finally sprang for an upgrade and, since I was already upgrading on image quality, I decided to upgrade the size, too: I bought a 65-inch LG evo C4, which is the company’s mid-range unit released in 2024.

At first, the experience was amazing. The television rendered colors and shadows wonderfully and, seeing as one of the goals with this purchase was to indulge my physical media habit, I began running through my collection of 4K Blu-ray discs with the madcap energy of a true fanatic.

However, things took a bit of an unexpected turn when, midway through “McCabe and Mrs. Miller,” I was suddenly overcome by a wave of nausea. I’m not particularly sensitive to motion sickness, but this sensation — which made it feel vaguely like I was going to hurl — persisted for several hours after it initially began. It was then replaced by a small tension headache.

I discovered that this is actually a somewhat common experience for new OLED adopters. Indeed, Reddit is rife with posts from new television owners who claim they feel like their big new toy is breaking their brain.

“I got the tv yesterday and still feel sick today,” one Redditor, who said they had recently purchased an LG C2, wrote. “Feel light headed and nauseous a day later. Thinking about taking it back. Is this normal? I’m scared to turn the thing on lol.”

Others blamed the sheer size of the screen. One guy, who bought an 85-inch TLC, claimed it had led his wife to the conclusion that “it’s too big and say that she feels sick watching. Is that a thing that a screen can be too big?”

There doesn’t seem to be a consensus on why this happens. Many Redditors blame certain motion-smoothing settings. However, my TV did not come with those settings enabled. Others blamed viewers for sitting too close to the screen — yet I was sitting a solid nine feet away, which is well within the recommended range for a 65-inch screen.

Finally, others have argued that the screen brightness could be agitating users’ eyes. I dialed down the brightness on mine to around 50 percent, although I had doubts as to whether this actually had anything to do with the feelings I was having.

In considering my nausea, one theory that sprang to mind was that it might just be my eyes’ inexperience with viewing such a big screen. The TV was so large that it often felt like my eye had to trace different parts of the screen to take in the whole picture and, if the scene involved significant motion (most movie scenes do, after all), it conjured the sensation of trying to stare too intently at something out the window of a moving car.

After a few days, however, my eyes finally adjusted. The nausea was gone. All that remained was an immense and beautiful home viewing experience that made every previous viewing experience pale by comparison.

Initial physiological reactions aside, the size of the 65-inch screen (and whether your living space actually has room for it) is still something that needs to be considered carefully by potential buyers. I recently moved into a place with a slightly bigger living room, which has given me the flexibility to install a bigger device. At my old apartment, however, this size of TV would have definitely felt like it was devouring the space.

Another slight frustration is that the C4 does not come with any detailed installation instructions. The screen (which is so wide it’s difficult to move without another person there to help you) comes detached from its base, and the user is just sort of expected to figure out how to effectively move and put together the two pieces. A quick YouTube video is all that is necessary to understand this process, but you have to be careful when moving and assembling the pieces so as not to scratch or damage the screen.

Once the whole thing is set up and assembled, the OLED is a truly beautiful thing to behold. The customization that’s possible, including advanced brightness and color control — and things like “Filmmaker Mode” (which claims to adjust each movie’s color and frame rate settings to those intended by the director) — make the user experience really powerful.

To sum up: The evo C4 is a really spectacular piece of equipment that has a lot to offer the avid home entertainment viewer — although there may be a bit of a learning curve before it makes your cinema dreams come true.

#198. Germany news: IG Metall union calls for new 24-hour strike

Germany's biggest single union, IG Metall, is calling on car and shipyard workers to strike amid a pay row. Meanwhile, Germany's president is setting off on an Africa trip. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of headlines from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:

Bosses at soccer team Bayern Munich have publicly questioned whether young Germany international Jamal Musiala's contract is valid in view of a debilitating neurological condition.

The remarks have been criticized by media and from several other quarters, among them the global players' union FIFPRO, which accused the officials of neglecting their "duty of care" toward their players.

You can read details on what has been happening at the top football club in this DW article: Bayern Munich bosses under fire over Jamal Musiala comments

Friedrich Christian "Mick" Flick, an art collector, investor and multimillionaire who belonged to one of Germany's richest business dynasties, has died aged 82 in Rosenheim in the southern state of Bavaria, his family has said.

The family said in a statement issued on Saturday that Flick left behind "the memory of a life shaped by significant acts of generosity as a donor and patron, particularly in contemporary art and in promoting tolerance."

Flick was the grandson of Friedrich Flick, who made a huge fortune in the Nazi era with his coal and steel business, partly by using forced labor.

This past came back to haunt the grandson in 2003 when he pledged to loan his world-famous collection of modern art to Berlin, with the Central Council of Jews in Germany calling the Flick Collection a "Göring Collection" and saying the loan was intended to wash clean the "blood money" from the Nazi era.

The collection, which contains some 2,500 works by 150 artists, was exhibited in parts in the German capital from 2004 to 2021.

Flick later said in an interview that the widespread outrage, while hurtful, had forced him to look more closely at his family's history.

According to his family, Flick once said: "I have no guilt for my forefathers' conduct, but I feel a responsibility, a very special responsibility. Every German bears this responsibility. As a Flick, I bear it twice."

Among other things, he collaborated with the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which oversees Berlin's museums, to research his family's Nazi past.

He also set up a foundation in Potsdam, near Berlin, that aimed to combat xenophobia and racism and contributed €5 million ($5.4 million) to the foundation to compensate former forced laborers.

The family was also involved in a highly publicized party donations scandal in the 1980s that became known as the "Flick Affair."

"Mick" Flick married Countess Maya von Schönburg (1958-2019), the older sister of well-known socialite, businesswoman, art collector and artist Gloria von Thurn und Taxis, in 1985. The couple had three children.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is setting off on a five-day trip to Africa that will take him to Ivory Coast, Ghana and Kenya.

Steinmeier will be accompanied by a business delegation and is expected to focus on economic cooperation and the training of skilled workers during the trip.

On Monday, Steinmeier is to be received by Ivorian President Allassane Outtara in Abidjan, Ivory Coast's largest city and seat of government.

The next day, in the Ghanaian capital, Accra, he is set to open the German-African Business Summit, which, according to its website, "brings together senior business executives, policymakers, investors, and industry leaders from across Germany and Africa."

On Wednesday, he will be received by Kenyan President William Ruto in Nairobi.

In Kenya, Steinmeier will also visit the Crescent Island Game Sanctuary on Thursday, the last day of his trip.

The Federal Institute for Hydrology (BfG) has said it expects water levels in large rivers in western Germany, including the Rhine, to return to average or above in the next few days amid sustained rainfall.

It said the water level at the key gauge in Kaub near Koblenz, located at an important bottleneck on the Middle Rhine, could reach some 3.3 meters (10.8 feet), more than 3 meters higher than the last recorded low-water readings.

The BfG said it also expected rising water levels in the Weser and Danube rivers, with smaller increases in the Elbe and Oder.

The rising water level in the Rhine, an important shipping route, means that conditions for water-borne cargo transport have improved, according to Germany's inland navigation association BDB.

"The more abundant rainfall in the past days has caused the water level in the Rhine to rise considerably, and they will keep rising a great deal in the next few days as well, meaning that each ship has much more transport capacity again," said Fabian Spiess, the deputy manager at BDB.

In the middle of the year, many ships were forced to drastically reduce the loads they carried, leading to economic losses that will not be recuperated any time soon, according to Spiess.

He cited the year 2018, in which shipping on the Rhine was also hindered by extremely low water levels, saying that the months of improved conditions at the end of that year had not been enough to make good the economic damage incurred.

The conservation NGO also said that the current rain provided temporary relief to the environment but could not compensate for the negative consequences of the long dry period.

It said species of animals, such as amphibians and water insects, that lived in small bodies of water and moist habitats had been particularly impacted.

Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig says that she intends to tighten the law on murders committed with "gender-specific" motives, with a particular focus on femicides perpetrated by men who are unable to accept a separation or the desire of a woman to live a self-determined life.

"A man kills, or attempts to kill, his partner or ex-partner almost every day in Germany," Hubig told the Sunday edition of the mass-circulation Bild newspaper.

"Any man killing a woman because she wants to leave him must be punished as a murderer," she said, noting that in some cases, courts cite a man's deep sadness or fear of losing a partner to someone else as extenuating circumstances. This can lead to a lesser conviction of manslaughter.

She said that in future, courts should look more closely at such motives to determine whether they were based on sentiments of patriarchal possessiveness.

However, Hubig, who belongs to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), said she was opposed to making femicide a separate category of crime, as some women's rights organizations have demanded.

She said that, in her opinion, doing so would have "no advantages over what we are intending — and much bigger disadvantages."

The proposals are currently being debated within the coalition government and are expected to be presented to the states and associations for consideration before the end of the year.

They will then have to go before the Cabinet before being put before the parliament.

A new goal celebration was devised by Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha after his previous one caused controversy due to its religious aspect.

After scoring the goal that secured Dortmund's 1-0 victory over Borussia Mönchengladbach (see entry below), Nmecha knelt on one knee and crossed his arms in front of his chest. He then spread his arms, appearing to pray with his eyes closed.

Nmecha told broadcaster Sky that he intends to continue expressing his faith during goal celebrations, adding that he had once again given glory to Jesus.

However, he did not perform the controversial part of his usual goal celebration. In it, he removes an imaginary crown from his head and places it on the pitch in front of him while kneeling.

This celebration has been heavily criticized, even by Dortmund's fan department.

Nmecha explained that the celebrations is about "putting down my 'crown' in front of the soon-to-come king and point out to Jesus, my hope and my strength."

The gesture is used by Ballers in God, a network of Christian football players that has been criticized for the homophobic and queerphobic statements made by its members.

Dortmund president Hans-Joachim Watzke said he asked the player not to do the celebration again.

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha led his team to the top of the German Bundesliga table with a 1-0 victory over last-place Borussia Mönchengladbach.

Meanwhile, Bayern Munich was held to a 1-1 draw at home by Cologne on Friday, and striker Harry Kane suffered a serious ankle injury. The Ballon d'Or winner is set to miss several months after undergoing ankle surgery earlier on Saturday.

Now, Dortmund has 24 points after 10 games, putting them two points ahead of Bayern and third-place Freiburg, who defeated Elversberg 1-0.
